title: MoMA Money Map
kick: Case study, New York. From the research brief of 28 September 2026.
summary: Public money is a rounding error in MoMA's operating budget: reported government grants were $49,965 in FY2020, $20,000 in FY2021, a one-off $10M federal Shuttered Venue grant in FY2022, and nothing after.

The public relationship is structural instead. New York City put $65M into the 2004 building, about $700M of tax-exempt bonds went through a state public-benefit corporation, and Museum Tower's property taxes are diverted to MoMA-related bonds.
The contested money sits on the board: two trustees with Epstein ties, several of the largest Republican donors in the country, and the founders of BlackRock, Citadel, Apollo and KKR.
bullets: Leon Black paid Epstein $158M to $170M in 2012 to 2017, stepped down as Chair in 2021 and remains a trustee; Senator Ron Wyden, ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, ran an inquiry from 2023 to 2026.
Glenn Dubin, a trustee, appears in Epstein flight logs and was subpoenaed by the US Virgin Islands in 2020; he denies wrongdoing.
Pfizer and Johnson & Johnson are $25,000-tier members every year since FY2016; MoMA honoured Pfizer's CEO in 2021 and Pfizer gave $100,000.
Vice Chair Maja Oeri holds about 7.5% of Roche voting shares; trustee Jon Stryker is heir to Stryker medical devices.
Strike MoMA ran ten weeks in 2021 and named Black, Dubin, Tananbaum, Cohen and Fink.
In the Cold War, MoMA staff moved between the museum, Rockefeller's wartime agency and the CIA's cultural fronts; direct CIA funding of MoMA is not documented.

title: Epstein and the arts: the cross-reference
kick: Case study. 61 links to 51 institutions, each checked against its sources, from the DOJ file releases of 2025 and 2026.
summary: We traced every documented tie between Jeffrey Epstein and a cultural institution: trustees, directors, donors, gifts and venues. A second researcher checked each link against its sources, and links were corrected or dropped where the sources fell short.

A link puts the Epstein-linked flag on a pin when it is documented and runs through money or leadership: Epstein's own gifts, or a trustee, patron, director, dean or donor with documented dealings with him. Visits, loans, guest engagements and mentions in the files are listed on the pin without changing its grade. Alleged and denied links are marked as such.

Most links run through a few trustees and donors whose money sits on several boards at once: Leon Black, Glenn Dubin, Ronald Lauder, Les Wexner, Thomas Pritzker and Steve Tisch. Epstein's own gifts went mostly to schools and programmes, among them Interlochen, the New York Academy of Art, Bard, Hasty Pudding, the MIT Media Lab and Poetry in America.

Leaders left the MIT Media Lab, the School of Visual Arts, the Institut du monde arabe and Bard. English National Ballet, the Royal Philharmonic and the Amandus Festival dropped their patrons. Black and Dubin are still MoMA trustees, and the Wexner Center still carries the name.

cells: Crown Princess Mette-Marit had been high patron of the Amandus Festival, a youth film festival in Lillehammer, since 2006. Emails from 2011 to 2014 in the Epstein files show extensive contact between her and Epstein.

On 28 April 2026 the festival's board voted unanimously to end the patronage, saying it had become "mer forstyrrende enn styrkende" (more disturbing than strengthening). She said she understood the decision.

Thomas Pritzker is a former chairman of the Art Institute of Chicago. DOJ files show contact with Epstein from 2000 to 2018, planned visits to Epstein's island and advice on staffing it. Pritzker kept in contact with Epstein after the 2008 conviction, and he denies the allegation Virginia Giuffre made against him in a 2016 deposition unsealed in January 2024.
Pritzker stepped down as Hyatt executive chairman on 16 February 2026, saying he deeply regrets the association.
Association pour la promotion de la politique culturelle nationale conduite dans les années 80 et 90 du XXe siècle

Epstein's charity Gratitude America gave $57,897 in 2018 to this Paris nonprofit, which was launched the same year. POLITICO found it had barely existed beyond some basic paperwork. Its president and treasurer were Jack Lang's former chiefs of staff, and Lang told POLITICO in October 2020 that the money was meant to finance a film.

Epstein's foundation Enhanced Education paid $250,000 to the Origins Project, headed by Lawrence Krauss at Arizona State University, between December 2010 and April 2017. Krauss organised an Epstein-funded 2006 gravity conference in the US Virgin Islands and kept taking Epstein's money after his 2008 conviction.
The project closed in 2018, and ASU returned $25,000 in unspent money to Enhanced Education.

Bard president Leon Botstein flew with Leon Black and his wife on their plane to the Virgin Islands, where the Blacks hosted a fundraising dinner on their boat with Epstein present; Bard dates the trip to 2012, and University World News to December 2018. Botstein says the trip led to a $250,000 gift from Black for the arts at Bard about 18 months later. Black paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017, according to a 2021 Dechert review for Apollo.

Leon Botstein, Bard's president from 1975 to 2026, pursued Epstein as a donor from 2012 to 2019, and Epstein gave to Bard through his foundation Enhanced Education in 2011 and 2012. Epstein attended concerts at Bard's Fisher Center. In 2016 Epstein's foundation Gratitude America paid Botstein a $150,000 consulting fee, which he says he passed on to Bard, and WilmerHale found he visited Epstein's townhouse about 25 times and his island for two days between 2012 and 2019.

A WilmerHale review commissioned by Bard's trustees found Botstein knew of Epstein's crimes in 2012, did not tell Bard the gifts came from Epstein, and "minimized and was not fully accurate" about the relationship; it found nothing illegal. On 1 May 2026 Botstein announced he would retire as president at the end of June 2026.

Leon and Debra Black gave $48 million toward the arts centre, which opened in 2012. Epstein had been a director of the Black Family Foundation, through which the gifts passed; he is still listed on its 2012 tax forms, which the Blacks call an error, saying he left in 2007. Black paid Epstein $158 million to $170 million from 2012 to 2017 and denies knowing of Epstein's crimes.
The centre has not been renamed. In June 2026, after community calls to rename it, the trustees set up an ad hoc naming committee.

Jean Pigozzi, who founded the CAAC – The Pigozzi Collection of contemporary African art, corresponded with Epstein in 2013 about women's physical attributes, according to DOJ files released on 30 January 2026. He also emailed "Gmax", whom ARTnews takes to be Ghislaine Maxwell. Pigozzi does not deny the correspondence and says he regrets meeting Epstein and Ghislaine.
Pigozzi called the emails "stupid" and said he "never had anything to do with him and girls".

The New York Times reported that one of Black's art companies sold Braque's Le Guéridon for $5 million to a trust Epstein controlled, as part of Black's tax-deferral exchange. Christie's sold a Le Guéridon on 15 May 2017 for $10.1 million as "property of an important private collector", but Braque painted several works with that title and no source says the trust consigned it. Black paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017, according to a 2021 Dechert review for Apollo.

In September 2018 Epstein emailed Jack Lang and his daughter Caroline about a venue for the 2019 Pritzker Architecture Prize ceremony, writing that Pritzker wanted "something unique this time". The ceremony was held at the Palace of Versailles in May 2019; nothing shows Epstein arranged it. Pritzker, whose family runs the prize, kept writing to Epstein after his 2008 conviction and has said he "exercised terrible judgment in maintaining contact".
Pritzker stepped down as Hyatt executive chairman on 16 February 2026.

In 2014 executive director Peter Doroshenko asked Epstein to lend "Below", a Richard Phillips painting Epstein owned, for Phillips' solo show "Negation of the Universe". Epstein's assistant Lesley Groff replied that he was not interested, and the emails show no closer relationship.
Doroshenko says he did not know who Epstein was.
Peter Mandelson chaired the Design Museum's trustees until June 2023. He was removed as UK ambassador to the US in 2025 over emails on his Epstein ties, and left the Labour Party in February 2026.
He left the Labour Party in February 2026.

Alexander Maxwell Djerassi has been a Djerassi trustee since 2017 and is now board secretary. An itinerary in the DOJ files lists him and fellow trustee Michael Molesky as guests at a "Mindshift Conference" on the weekend of 7 January 2011, with events on St. Thomas and on Epstein's island, Little St. James. He is Ghislaine Maxwell's nephew, and he says of the 2011 lunch, speaking for himself and Molesky, "We had no awareness of Epstein's heinous crimes."

Both men remain on the board. The residency calls the 2011 visit a "social lunch" years before they joined the board and says it had no ties to Epstein or Maxwell. The 2011 visit came six years before they joined the board, so under the visits rule it adds no flag.

Edge's IRS filings show foundations linked to Epstein gave $638,000 of the nearly $857,000 Edge received from 2001 to 2017; his last recorded gift was $30,000 in 2015. Epstein attended Edge's "billionaires' dinners", the last of which was in March 2015. Brockman, a literary agent to scientists, brought Epstein into contact with scientists, and Epstein's money made Edge's exclusive events possible.
Edge removed photos of Epstein from its website. Brockman did not answer BuzzFeed News.

Prince Andrew was patron of English National Ballet for 18 years. ENB accepted his resignation "with immediate effect" on 22 November 2019, after his Newsnight interview about Epstein, and some ENB trustees had joined calls for him to go. A longtime friend of Epstein, he was arrested on 19 February 2026 on suspicion of misconduct in public office, over whether he passed confidential trade-envoy reports to Epstein, and has not been charged.

DOJ files released in January 2026 show Epstein advised Black's lawyers on the purchase of Picasso's 1931 sculpture Buste de Femme (Marie-Thérèse) from Gagosian for $115 million, negotiated in 2015; the work went to Black after a legal settlement made public in early 2016. In 2012 Epstein also worked with lawyers on a proposed exchange of Black's $46 million 1961 Rothko for a $48 million Picasso held by Gagosian, and the documents do not show whether it happened. Black paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017, according to a 2021 Dechert review for Apollo.
Gagosian did not respond to ARTnews.

GBH presented Elisa New's Poetry in America from its 2018 premiere until 2022. Epstein gave $110,000 in 2016 to Verse Video Education, the nonprofit that produces the show. New and Epstein emailed from 2013 to 2018 about support for her projects.

GBH says it fully cut ties in 2023, while New's spokesperson says she left GBH herself in 2022. GBH says it was "not aware of any Epstein financial contributions to the series"; New's spokesperson says the money paid for educational content, not episodes, and none went to GBH. PBS cut ties with the show in December 2025.

Harvard's May 2020 report found Epstein gave $9.1 million from 1998 to 2008, including $6.5 million in 2003 to create the Program for Evolutionary Dynamics (PED). Epstein visited PED's offices more than 40 times between 2010 and 2018. Nowak, PED's director, kept a relationship with Epstein for 15 years, including after his release from prison, and gave him access to PED's offices.

Harvard sanctioned Nowak in 2021 for breaking its rules on professional conduct, campus access and endorsements, and shut PED down. Harvard gave $200,937 in unspent funds to My Life My Choice and GEMS.

The Jeffrey Epstein Virgin Islands Foundation and Gratitude America gave the Hasty Pudding Institute of 1770, the umbrella group for Hasty Pudding Theatricals, at least $375,000: $75,000 in 2013 and $50,000 a year from 2014 to 2019. The Pudding listed Epstein as a 2018 "Guardian of the Sphinx" donor.

In 2019 members petitioned the board to give the money to anti-trafficking groups. The Pudding removed Epstein's name from its donor page and gave $50,000 to an anti-trafficking nonprofit. Chairman Andrew Farkas says Epstein had no tie to the Pudding beyond giving money.

Jack Lang led the Institut du monde arabe from 2013. He is named more than 600 times in the DOJ files released on 30 January 2026, and emails show he travelled in Epstein's jet and car. Lang, a former French culture minister, was introduced to Epstein by Woody Allen, called him "a generous sponsor" and exchanged messages with him from 2012 to 2019.

Lang resigned as president on 7 February 2026. The day before, the Paris prosecutor had opened a preliminary investigation into him and his daughter Caroline for laundering of aggravated tax fraud. Both deny wrongdoing.

Epstein attended Interlochen's summer camp in 1967 and gave money to it from 1990 to 2003, including a $200,000 gift, acknowledged in February 1994, for a lodge on Green Lake named after him. A witness at Ghislaine Maxwell's 2021 trial and a second woman say Epstein and Maxwell met them at the camp at 13 and 14, from 1994, and DOJ files show the pair met a student alone at the lodge.

Interlochen renamed the building Green Lake Lodge in 2009 and says reviews in 2009 and 2019 found no evidence of crimes on campus. In May 2026 it announced it would tear the lodge down. In July 2026 a Sanghavi Law Office report recorded two women's accounts that Epstein engaged in sexual conduct with them, one of them at the lodge.

A 2014 spreadsheet in the DOJ Epstein release, titled "Leon Black/ Narrows South East Asian Art Inventory", lists a $7 million Shiva that Bloomberg says fits the description of a piece tied to Douglas Latchford. In 2013 letters Bloomberg obtained, Latchford wrote to London dealer John Eskenazi about a similar bronze he supplied for Eskenazi to sell to Black. Black paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017, according to a 2021 Dechert review for Apollo.
Black's representatives say he "never met nor acquired anything directly from Latchford" and bought his few Cambodian works through a reputable dealer.

Steve Tisch is a LACMA trustee and in 2011 helped fund its purchase of Marclay's The Clock. Emails from April and May 2013 in the DOJ files show Epstein offering to introduce him to women. Tisch says they had a "brief association" and emailed about adult women, movies, philanthropy and investments, that he never went to the island, and that he deeply regrets associating with Epstein.

Chaslin was due to return to the Metropolitan Opera the next season after a 17-year absence. His emails with Epstein are in the DOJ files. Chaslin is linked to at least 376 DOJ documents going back to 2012 and says his contact with Epstein was trivial.
Slippedisc reported on 19 February 2026 that the Met withdrew its contract offer over the emails; it cites no statement from the Met.

The Metropolitan Opera was among the charities listed in the Jeffrey Epstein VI Foundation's press releases or IRS filings from 2010 to 2017. In July 2019 NBC News reported that the Met Opera was among 10 organisations with no record of any donation from Epstein or his foundation.

Peter Mahler sat on the Milwaukee Symphony Orchestra's 35-member board until February 2026. FOX6 first reported his Epstein link on 9 February 2026. The Epstein files show Mahler worked as a recruiter for Epstein in 2013, when Epstein was looking for an assistant, and Mahler calls the allegations against Epstein "abhorrent".
Mahler resigned from the board. On 13 February 2026 the orchestra said it had accepted his resignation and that the matter was unrelated to his board service.

Joi Ito wrote in an email that a $2 million gift from Bill Gates to the Media Lab was "directed by Jeffrey Epstein", while MIT's gift record said only that Gates gave on the recommendation of a friend who wished to remain anonymous. Gates's spokesperson says any claim that Epstein directed his grantmaking is "completely false". Gates met Epstein at least once to discuss philanthropy, and media reports of flight records allege he flew on Epstein's jet from New Jersey to Palm Beach in March 2013.

MIT's Goodwin Procter review (January 2020) found Epstein gave MIT $850,000 in 10 gifts from 2002 to 2017, nine of them after his 2008 conviction, including $525,000 to the Media Lab under director Joi Ito. The New Yorker reported that Epstein arranged at least $7.5 million in donations to the Lab and that the Lab logged his gifts as anonymous, while MIT's donor database marked him "disqualified". Ito solicited and accepted Epstein's post-conviction gifts to the Media Lab and hosted his visits, and he also took $1.2 million from Epstein for his own investment funds.
Ito resigned on 7 September 2019. MIT committed $850,000 to survivor charities and put Seth Lloyd on paid leave.

Reid Hoffman met Epstein at the MIT Media Lab in July 2013, and in 2014 he went to Epstein's island for a fundraising event that Joi Ito says he requested. Their last known in-person meeting was a 2015 dinner Hoffman hosted, and Epstein emailed him in 2017. Hoffman says he dealt with Epstein only for Media Lab fundraising.
Hoffman apologised in September 2019 for having "helped to repair his reputation".

Glenn Dubin is a MoMA trustee, and the New York Post reported in October 2019 that MoMA had named a fourth-floor gallery after him and his wife, Eva Andersson-Dubin. In September 2020 the US Virgin Islands attorney general gave notice that she would subpoena him, and he was named in documents unsealed in January 2024. Eva Andersson-Dubin is Epstein's ex-girlfriend, and Virginia Giuffre alleged that Epstein trafficked her to Dubin in 2001, when she was 16, which the Dubins categorically deny.
In November 2019 the Guerrilla Girls called for Dubin and Leon Black to be removed from the board and for their galleries to be draped in black. MoMA did not comment.

Leon Black is a MoMA trustee and was its board chair until 2021. DOJ files show Epstein guided his $115 million purchase of Picasso's Buste de Femme (Marie-Thérèse) from Gagosian, a sculpture shown in MoMA's 2015 "Picasso Sculpture" show. Black paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017, according to a 2021 Dechert review for Apollo, or $170 million for tax and estate planning by Senator Ron Wyden's count, and he denies the sexual abuse allegations against him.

Black stepped down as chair in 2021 and is still a MoMA trustee in 2026. In 2023 he paid the US Virgin Islands $62.5 million to settle Epstein-related claims; the settlement notes he was not accused of wrongdoing.

Ronald Lauder is a former MoMA board chair and is still a trustee. He is mentioned more than 900 times in the DOJ files released in January 2026, including a 2014 email that sent Epstein the possession and loan agreement for a Kurt Schwitters work Lauder co-owns with Leon Black. In 2017 Lauder's and Epstein's assistants arranged meetings and calls, and Epstein's assistant said Epstein wanted to see two years of Lauder's tax returns and his will; ARTnews found no direct communication between the two men.
Lauder has not commented publicly, and his representative did not respond to ARTnews.

In an 18 March 2012 email in the DOJ's January 2026 release, Epstein wrote that "the govt is going to open the musee dorsay for me and woody alien at 4", "alien" being his typo for Woody Allen. He later bragged about the visit in emails, including one to Eva Dubin.
The Musée d'Orsay did not respond to ARTnews and has not confirmed the visit.

Black lent his Van Gogh "Quarry near Saint-Rémy", valued at $60 million in 2016, to the Orsay's 2014 show "Van Gogh/Artaud: Le Suicidé de la Société". The Art Newspaper reports that the Epstein files indicate his Van Goghs were collateral for large bank loans around 2016. Epstein gave Black "extensive financial advice" for fees of at least $158 million, and Black denies wrongdoing and says he knew nothing of Epstein's crimes until 2019.

Ronald Lauder founded the Neue Galerie, which says it co-owns Kirchner's Berlin Street Scene with a private collection. ARTnews describes a 2016 document in the DOJ files as a list of Leon Black's art holdings, including a 50% stake in a Kirchner of that name valued at about $50 million, but it does not confirm that Black is the museum's co-owner. Lauder is mentioned more than 900 times in the January 2026 files, where his and Epstein's assistants arranged meals and calls in 2017; ARTnews found no direct communication between the two men.

Eileen Guggenheim was the Academy's dean in 1995 and later its board chair. Emails show that after Epstein's 2008 conviction she encouraged his support of the school, and in 2014 he gave $30,000 for scholarships at her invitation. Maria Farmer alleges that Guggenheim introduced her to Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell at her 1995 thesis show, pressed her to sell Epstein a painting at a steep discount and ignored her complaints; Guggenheim denies "the substance and odious implications" of the allegations.

The Academy commissioned a report that disputed Farmer's claims. In March 2026 it said it should not have taken Epstein's money or let him attend events, and Guggenheim brought her retirement forward by a month, to April 2026.

Epstein sat on the Academy's board from 1987 to 1994 and met student Maria Farmer there in 1995; Farmer reported him to the FBI in 1996, the first report against him. After his 2008 conviction he bought a $25,000 table at the Academy's Tribeca Ball in 2012 and in 2014, gave $30,000 for scholarship support in 2014, and attended Academy events.
In March 2026 the Academy admitted "serious failures", said it would give $65,900 linked to the 2012 and 2014 events to GEMS, and set up an ethics committee. It had given GEMS $30,000 in 2020.
Crown Princess Mette-Marit was patron of the Norwegian Library Association. Emails from 2011 to 2014 in the Epstein files show extensive contact between her and Epstein.
The association put her patronage on pause on 9 February 2026 over the Epstein revelations and ended it on 17 March 2026.
NYU Tisch School of the Arts

Steve Tisch sits on the Dean's Council of NYU Tisch School of the Arts, named after a 1982 donation from his father and uncle. DOJ files show emails from 2013 to 2017 in which Epstein described women to him, including an April 2013 thread titled "Ukrainian Girl". Todd Meister introduced Tisch to Epstein in April 2013, and Tisch says the emails were about "adult women", movies, philanthropy and investments, that he never went to the island, and that he deeply regrets the association.
NYU did not respond to requests for comment.

cells: In June 2013 Chaslin emailed Epstein, "I found the right person for your private visit", and called his contact "the best one at the Paris Opera". In a March 2026 letter he says Epstein's secretary asked him for a woman translator for a visit to the Paris Opera and Versailles with Woody Allen, and the woman he proposed declined. Chaslin is linked to at least 376 DOJ documents going back to 2012, and he asked Epstein to arrange a meeting with Woody Allen.
Chaslin says the visit was "purely cultural" and that he received no money. He is not accused of wrongdoing.

Black bought the art-book publisher Phaidon in 2012. The Guerrilla Girls say they signed with Phaidon in 2018 and broke the contract in 2019 over Black's Epstein ties, then published with Chronicle Books in 2020. An Apollo review found Black paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017 and found no evidence that he took part in Epstein's crimes.

Caroline Lang presided over Pictanovo's economic support fund for films and series until 4 February 2026. Pictanovo is an association funded by the Hauts-de-France region. She co-owned Prytanee LLC, a US Virgin Islands company created in 2016, with Epstein, and an Epstein will document names her for $5 million.

She stepped down on 4 February 2026 after the US Justice Department released the Epstein emails. France's National Financial Prosecutor (PNF) has opened a preliminary inquiry into her and Jack Lang on suspicion of laundering aggravated tax fraud.

Epstein's foundation Gratitude America gave $110,000 in 2016 to Verse Video Education, the nonprofit behind Elisa New's Poetry in America, and New and Epstein emailed about funding her projects from 2013 to at least 2018, including a possible $500,000 donation. Harvard gave the nonprofit office space and paid part of its staff salaries. New, a former Harvard professor married to Larry Summers, told the Boston Globe she did not know about Harvard's 2008 ban on Epstein gifts when she took the 2016 donation.
GBH ended its ties with the show in 2023, and PBS stopped distributing it in December 2025. Harvard opened an investigation into New and Summers.

Emails released in November 2025 show Epstein brokered a donation of an unspecified amount from Leon Black to Elisa New, which Harvard did not disclose. New wrote to Epstein in 2015 that "The Leon Black gift changed everything for me last year", tying it to her Poetry in America project. Black paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017, according to a 2021 Dechert review for Apollo.
PBS stopped distributing Poetry in America in December 2025.

Tom Pritzker runs the Hyatt Foundation, which is behind the Pritzker Architecture Prize. Unredacted DOJ files show frequent contact with Epstein after his 2008 plea deal. Pritzker said he "exercised terrible judgment in maintaining contact" with Epstein and Maxwell, and he denies Virginia Giuffre's allegation against him in her 2016 deposition.
Pritzker retired as Hyatt executive chairman in February 2026 but kept his role at the prize foundation. Archinect reported on 24 February 2026 that the prize would delay its 2026 announcement.
Prytanee LLC (art fund for young artists)

Epstein set up Prytanee LLC in the US Virgin Islands in 2016, Caroline Lang held 50% of its shares, and $1.4 million was credited to it to buy artworks. Lang calls it a legal fund for buying work by young artists. Caroline Lang, Jack Lang's daughter, was promised $5 million in a will Epstein signed two days before his death in 2019.

France's financial prosecutor (PNF) opened a preliminary investigation into Jack and Caroline Lang for laundering of aggravated tax fraud on 6 February 2026. Caroline Lang says she received no pay or benefit from the fund and did not know about the bequest, which she never received. Jack Lang's lawyer says Jack Lang never received a cent.
Epstein joined Rockefeller University's board of trustees in 2000. A university trustee list names "Mr. Jeffrey Epstein, President, J. Epstein & Company".
He left the board after one term. A board spokesperson said he did not have enough time to commit.

Prince Andrew was the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra's patron, and the orchestra thanked him for his support "over the past 15 years". In November 2019 its board decided to "part company with its patron, with immediate effect". A longtime friend of Epstein, he lost his royal titles in October 2025 and was arrested on 19 February 2026 on suspicion of misconduct in public office over what the Epstein files disclosed; he has not been charged.

Frédéric Chaslin got a three-year contract as Santa Fe Opera's chief conductor in 2010 and left abruptly in 2012, a year early. Emails show Epstein went backstage and sat in the front row at a Tosca there, and board member Peter Frank emailed both men in 2014. Chaslin met Epstein about a year after Epstein's release in July 2009 and is named nearly 400 times in the DOJ files, including a 2013 email offering "a great girl for your next stay in Paris", who he says was to be a translator.
The opera says it "does not comment on individual personnel matters". Chaslin has not been charged.

Ross chaired SVA's MFA Art Practice department from 2009. In October 2009 Epstein proposed a "statutory" exhibition of "girls and boys ages 14 - 25", and Ross replied, "You are incredible." Ross, a former director of the Whitney, SFMOMA and ICA Boston, stayed close friends with Epstein after his 2008 conviction, kept in contact until at least 2016 and says he contacted Epstein again in 2019.
SVA accepted his resignation, effective 3 February 2026, after a student petition.

In 2001, while David A. Ross was director, SFMOMA acquired a 20% interest in John F. Simon Jr.'s ComplexCity (2000), recorded as a "fractional and promised gift of Jeffrey Epstein". In 2009 director Neal Benezra wrote to thank Epstein for his "continued support".

SFMOMA says the 2009 letter was standard donor language and it has no record of support from Epstein after 2001. The work was never exhibited; the museum deaccessioned it in October 2019 and returned its share to the artist.

Oxman's Vespers II was shown in her 2022 SFMOMA exhibition "Nature x Humanity". Emails in the 2026 DOJ release show she thanked Epstein in 2017 for supporting her Vespers "death masks", and in December 2017 he agreed by email to give $25,000 toward a follow-on project. Epstein gave $125,000 to Oxman's MIT design lab in 2017, and she apologised in 2019.

The New York Times reported, from documents, that Black sold Giacometti's Figure Moyenne II for $25 million on 23 November 2016 to a trust Epstein controlled, as part of a tax-deferral exchange. Epstein's emails discuss Black's talks with Sotheby's, Christie's and Gagosian about buying an unnamed Giacometti, and Sotheby's sold a version of Figure Moyenne II in London on 21 June 2017 for £17.9 million, but no source says it was the trust's piece. Black paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017, according to a 2021 Dechert review for Apollo.

Caroline Lang became general delegate of the independent film and TV producers' union in January 2026 and resigned on 2 February 2026, about three weeks later. She resigned after Mediapart reported from the DOJ files that she held half the shares of Prytanee LLC, a company Epstein set up in the US Virgin Islands in 2016 with $1.4 million in its accounts. Lang, a film producer and Jack Lang's daughter, says she met Epstein through Woody Allen in 2012, and a will Epstein signed two days before his death names her for $5 million.

She says she never benefited from the company and did not know about the bequest, which she never received. The Paris prosecutor opened a preliminary investigation into her and her father for laundering of aggravated tax fraud.

Caroline Lang held roles at Séries Mania, the Lille TV-series festival. La Voix du Nord first reported that she had to give them up after the US Justice Department released Epstein's emails. She held 50% of Prytanee LLC, a company created with Epstein in the US Virgin Islands in 2016, a will Epstein signed promised her $5 million, and she says Woody Allen introduced her to Epstein in 2012.
She stood down on 4 February 2026, the same day she left Pictanovo. She calls Epstein an acquaintance and says she received no money or benefit.

Chaslin was engaged, without a formal signed contract, to conduct Verdi's "Aida" at Teatro Massimo from 22 to 31 May 2026. The DOJ files show a relationship with Epstein dating back to 2012. Chaslin corresponded with Epstein from 2012, including about #MeToo, and in 2013 recommended an interpreter for Epstein's Paris museum visits.

In March 2026 superintendent Marco Betta cancelled the engagement after the orchestra raised unease about Chaslin's ties to Epstein. Chaslin denies wrongdoing, says he "never received a single cent", and says a DOJ letter confirms he had no involvement.

Emails released by the DOJ show Epstein discussing paying a Baltic violin student's $15,000 Juilliard dorm costs and fixing her wire transfers, and in 2013-14 he asked Leon Botstein to assess her talent. Slippedisc calls Epstein a Juilliard donor at the time but gives no evidence, and The Daily Catch calls the student one of his victims.

The DOJ files released in January 2026 contain a copy of a $5,000 check dated 29 April 2014 from Enhanced Education, a foundation Epstein set up, made out to the Met for the Costume Institute Benefit (the Met Gala). Earlier, press releases from the Jeffrey Epstein VI Foundation listed the Met as receiving gifts from 2010 to 2012.

In July 2019 the Met told NBC News it had received no major donations from Epstein or his foundation, and that its only record was his purchase of tickets to two benefits in the early 1990s. The Met did not respond to ARTnews about the 2014 check, and ARTnews does not report whether the check was deposited.
links: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (The Met)

cells: OnStage Blog reports that a 2012 email chain in the DOJ's 30 January 2026 release shows the theatre's founder, Jeffrey Horowitz, approaching Epstein about a donation after Julie Taymor encouraged him to. The blog does not say whether a gift followed, and it says neither Taymor nor Horowitz is accused of wrongdoing. Taymor's name is also on an April 2009 Lion King ticket booking linked to Epstein or someone in his circle.
OnStage Blog asked for comment and reports no reply.

The Ohio State arts centre is named for Les Wexner's father and was founded with a 1987 gift from Les Wexner. Wexner is mentioned more than 1,000 times in the Epstein files. Epstein managed Wexner's money from 1989 to 2007 and held power of attorney over his fortune; Wexner denies an FBI listing of him as a co-conspirator and Virginia Giuffre's allegation that she was trafficked to him.

Ohio State has received about 500 renaming requests since Wexner's House Oversight deposition in February 2026 and says they are under review. title: What Democracy Now! reported
kick: Case study. 72 Democracy Now! stories from 2003 to 2026, each checked against an outside source.
summary: We read Democracy Now!'s reporting on who funds and controls cultural institutions, in the US and abroad, and checked every story against a second outlet or a primary document.

In the US the record runs from the Sackler and Kanders protests of 2019 to the federal moves on the arts after 2025: the Kennedy Center taken over, renamed and voted closed, a White House review of Smithsonian exhibitions, and federal money for public broadcasting ended.

Abroad, most stories are about attacks on culture rather than funding: the raid on the Freedom Theatre in Jenin, Osman Kavala's life sentence, jailed artists in Russia and Iran. They are listed here but do not change a grade, because the map grades who pays and who controls the money.

The record adds new pins for the Kennedy Center, three Smithsonian museums, Lincoln Center, the Eskenazi Museum of Art and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, and new flags on the Guggenheim, the Met, the Whitney, the American Museum of Natural History, the Noguchi Museum, the Science Museum and the National Air and Space Museum.

title: How tax breaks shape art sponsorship in Brazil
kick: Case study. What 20 studies say about the Rouanet Law, and a check of the 13 Brazilian pins against their own accounts.
summary: Since 1991, Brazil's Rouanet Law has let companies deduct the sponsorship of approved cultural projects from their income tax. The money is largely tax the state gives up, but the company chooses the project and puts its name on it.

The studies agree on where that money goes. It concentrates in São Paulo and Rio, in projects that are already successful, and in a small number of large sponsors, led by state-controlled firms such as Petrobras. Dekker calls the result control of the cultural sector by big business; network analysis of 2010 to 2014 finds some states 40% less likely to win sponsorship.
Contemporary art is the most unequal field. Silva (2025) finds its sponsorship more concentrated than music or theatre, because the field depends on large institutions and costly production.

This is the background to the Brazilian pins on the map. Petrobras, Vale and Ultra sponsor MASP, the Bienal de São Paulo, MAM Rio, MAM São Paulo, Inhotim and Casa França-Brasil. Their flags rest on who the sponsor is; Silva (2025) adds that corporate sponsorship of contemporary art in Brazil runs largely through the tax-incentive system, so much of it is paid for with public tax relief.

We checked the 13 Brazilian pins against their own audited accounts and annual reports, and against Salic data republished by Prosas; SalicNet itself sits behind a human check. Incentive-law money is 92% of Instituto Tomie Ohtake's 2024 revenue, 66% of MAM São Paulo's, 52% of MASP's operating revenue and 50 to 60% of Inhotim's budget, and 92% of MAM Rio's 2021 corporate sponsorship came through the three incentive laws. MASP was the largest Rouanet raiser in 2024. The state-run and levy-funded institutions (Sesc, MAM Bahia, Lasar Segall, FAAP, Casa França-Brasil) show no Rouanet money in open records.

That changes how to read the flags. Shell gave Inhotim R$7M through the law in 2024 (Salic data via Prosas), and half of Vale's R$400M ten-year deal with Inhotim runs through it. The oil and mining names are on the walls; much of the money behind them is tax the Brazilian state gave up.
bullets: The sponsor gets the name on the wall; the treasury pays much of the bill (Dekker 2019; Santos and de Paulo 2014).
State-owned companies are the biggest sponsors, which blurs the line between public and private support (Dekker and Rodrigues 2019).
Incentive-law spending is close to the culture ministry's own budget (Santos and de Paulo 2014).
Archives and poorer states get little; already successful projects get most (Balbino and Venâncio 2020; Pacheco and others 2026).

For 1993 to 2016, the law widened social, regional and genre inequalities. Gifts went to already successful projects and came mostly from large, often partly state-owned firms, acting as their tax cut.
The entangled political economy of Brazilian cultural policy: a case study of the Rouanet Law
Erwin Dekker and Anabela S. Rodrigues, 2019
The biggest sponsors are state-owned companies, which gain both a tax advantage and control over the cultural sector; the indirect subsidy ends up serving the sponsors.
Gastos tributários e recursos orçamentários nas políticas culturais
Eduardo Gomor dos Santos and Carla Beatriz de Paulo, 2014

Incentive-law spending rivals the culture ministry's own budget, concentrates in São Paulo and Rio and serves as marketing for large companies. Cultura Viva spreads money more evenly but is far smaller.
Network analysis of cultural funding in Brazil: uncovering regional differences and signatures
Across 106,804 transactions on 12,326 projects (2010 to 2014), funding tracks state wealth, and some states are 40% less likely to secure sponsorship.
Contribuições do patrocínio da Petrobras para o campo audiovisual de 1995 a 2007
Petrobras led film sponsorship through the federal incentive laws from 1995 to 2007, pulling other sponsors in and concentrating money in Rio de Janeiro.
Public and private art funding in Brazil
Sets the tax-incentive turn of the 1990s against Brazil's older pattern of narrow, unaccountable state patronage, and questions business enthusiasm on both sides.
As implicações das leis de incentivo à cultura sobre o processo de produção dos espetáculos no Theatro Municipal de São Paulo
Incentive-law money pushed the Theatro Municipal de São Paulo to run its productions on market principles.
Lei Rouanet: natureza do patrocínio quando não há fruição do benefício fiscal pelo patrocinador
Using the Monumenta Project, argues sponsorship money is private when the sponsor takes no tax benefit, against a Court of Auditors order to repay it.
Benefícios fiscais: proibição de vantagem em decorrência de patrocínio ou doação
Reads the Rouanet Law and two other incentive laws as barring sponsors from taking any advantage in return for a deductible sponsorship or donation.
Políticas culturais e arquivos públicos: o caso da Lei Rouanet
Giseli Milani Santiago Balbino and R. Venâncio, 2020
SalicNet data for 2010 to 2016 show Rouanet money for archives is negligible against the needs of Brazil's documentary heritage.
The economic impact of Brazil's cultural incentive policy
Luiz Gustavo Medeiros Barbosa and others, 2022
An input-output model of 2017 incentive-law projects puts their total economic impact at about US$198M.
A importância do Programa de Ação Cultural para incentivo da arte no Estado de São Paulo
Argues São Paulo state's ProAC, through public calls and a sales-tax credit, widens access and diversity.
Art and business: an international perspective on sponsorship
Collection on corporate arts support across the Americas, Europe and Asia, with a chapter by José Carlos Durand on Brazil.
Tax incentives for the cultural sector
Treats gift deductions in the US, Japan and Europe as indirect state support and weighs their pros and cons.
The paradox of corporate sponsorship of arts in the age of austerity
Funding cuts push museums toward sponsorship, which brings money but erodes artistic autonomy and can clash with a museum's mission.
Art, performance, and outsourcing in corporate art commissioning: an American scenario
Corporate commissioning trades on art's brand value and tax breaks, and imports art-world working habits into business.
Strategies and determinants of corporate support to the arts: insights from the Italian context
Italian firms back the arts for local legacy, social responsibility or market goals.
Determinants of the scale and sustainability of corporate sponsorship in arts
Larger firms, corporate foundations and consumer-facing firms give more, and sponsorship seen as authentic lasts longer.
Proposes legal changes to strengthen sponsorship contracts and argues a 10% tax exemption is too low to motivate sponsors.

title: Who connects the institutions
kick: Case study. 52 private funders and trustees each named at three or more institutions on the map, checked by hand, with 52 studies on how such networks work.
summary: This study reads the map's own records for private funders and trustees named at more than one institution, past or present. 52 of them reach three or more. Public bodies such as arts councils, the British Council, the Goethe-Institut, Pro Helvetia and the Mondriaan and Prince Claus funds are left out, because the question here is private money. Each link was checked by hand, and mentions that are not funding were removed.

Two networks show up. A philanthropic and banking layer links many institutions and carries few flags: the Warhol, Mellon, Luce and Ford foundations, Open Society, the Garfield Weston Foundation, and banks such as Bank of America, BBVA, UBS, JPMorgan and HSBC. A smaller group is flagged at every institution where it appears: Chevron (6), Baillie Gifford (6).

Bloomberg Philanthropies is the most widely shared private funder, at 55 institutions in 12 countries. 26 of them carry flags, mostly for other funders, because the map counts Bloomberg as a campaigned name only where activists targeted it at that institution.

Trustees and patrons connect institutions too. Ken Griffin and Citadel appear at 8, Leon Black at 5 and the Pritzker family at 5. The pair with the most funders in common is MASP and the Bienal de São Paulo, which share Bloomberg, Bradesco, Citi and Itaú.

Research on these networks points the same way. Cultural boards are small elite circles whose members sit on several boards, and a seat is part of their standing (Useem 1979; Ostrower 2002; O'Brien, Rees and Taylor 2022). Institutions at the centre of the web raise more money (King and Whitt 1997), and in England bodies tied to London boards hold more than double the funding income (O'Brien, Rees and Taylor 2022). Sponsors copy their peers in the same industry and city (Galaskiewicz and Burt 1991; Marquis and Tilcsik 2016), which is why the same names recur. Case studies of oil, bank and oligarch money show sponsorship used to buy legitimacy (Wu 2002; Evans 2015; Jones and others 2022; Michel and Szakonyi 2020).

Newer studies add three points. Cuts to public money push museums toward private sponsors (Proteau 2018; Rubio Aróstegui and Villarroya 2021; Aroles, Hassard and Hyde 2021). Protest can end a tie, as climate activists and artists did with BP at the National Portrait Gallery (Anguix-Vilches 2025), yet only about a third of institutions in one fundraiser sample had a donor policy (Rahwan and Leuker 2023), and tobacco money still draws little challenge (Solano 2024). Among US museums of American art, shared funders show up more often than shared trustees (Barabási and Shekhtman 2023).

The counts cover only funders the map names. Many institutions publish partial lists, so the real network is larger. Open any pin to see the funders it shares with others, and select a funder to show all its institutions on the globe.

cells: The Social Organization of the American Business Elite and Participation of Corporation Directors in the Governance of American Institutions
United States; 2,003 directors of the 797 largest corporations in 1969, followed into nonprofit (including cultural), government and business policy boards.

Directors who link several major corporations, the inner group, hold far more governing roles in other institutions. Their access to corporate resources and a shared social network explains part of this.
Early proof that the same business elites sit on many cultural boards.
Mozart in the Metropolis: The Arts Coalition and the Urban Growth Machine
United States; performing arts and city growth strategies, with examples from numerous cities.
Cities now use the performing arts as a growth strategy. An elite-sponsored political coalition promotes it, helped by changes in cities, the economy and the arts themselves.
Shows local elites back arts institutions as a coalition, not one by one.
The Museum Inc: Public Culture and the Sponsor
Museums under government pressure to raise money outside their budgets, in a 1989 article from an Australian journal.

Sponsorship was becoming a main new source of museum income, with costs that went uncounted. It was spreading with no ethical or policy rules, which the author says puts museum independence and the public's interest at risk.
An early sign that sponsor dependence was built by public funding pressure, decades before today's contested cases.
Corporate contributions officers rating nonprofit organisations that seek donations; the place is not named in the abstract I opened.

Giving officers' ratings of nonprofits spread through their network. The spread follows structural equivalence: officers in similar network positions rate alike, more than officers who simply talk to each other.
Shows sponsors adopt each other's favourites through the donor network, a core following mechanism.
Why the Wealthy Give: The Culture of Elite Philanthropy
New York City area; interviews with nearly one hundred wealthy donors.

Elite giving works as a way of life serving the class's social and cultural life, so educational and cultural causes are popular. Religion, ethnicity and gender pull some donors away from class-prestige giving.
Explains why wealthy donors favour museums and orchestras, and how giving binds elite groups.
What Do Interlocks Do? An Analysis, Critique, and Assessment of Research on Interlocking Directorates
Review of research on interlocking directorates in general; not specific to the arts.
Reviews why firms share directors and what those ties produce, weighs the two main criticisms of interlock research, and sets out directions for future work.
Standard review for judging what a shared-trustee link between two sponsors can and cannot show.
Princes and Paupers: Network Ties and Financial Contributions Among Nonprofit Arts Organizations
Karen N. King; J. Allen Whitt, 1997
Louisville, Kentucky, US; 25 local arts organisations inside a network of 149 organisations, firms and funding agencies built from almost 3,000 directors.
Arts organisations sitting more centrally in the web of shared directors draw more local contributions. Centrality links strongly to donations and only weakly to the organisation's own wealth.
Direct evidence that board overlap helps arts organisations attract donor money.
Trustees of Culture: Power, Wealth, and Status on Elite Arts Boards
United States; interviews with 76 trustees of two opera companies and two art museums.

Trustees weigh their own status against the needs of the big organisations they govern. Part of that status rests on board prestige, which keeps boards exclusive, though access and operations run more openly than expected.
Explains why wealthy people take arts board seats and why those boards stay closed.
Privatising Culture: Corporate Art Intervention since the 1980s
Britain and the United States; corporate involvement in the visual arts since the 1980s, including public arts agencies and museums.

Traces how policy shifts since the 1980s let corporations into the visual arts. Corporate takeover of museums gives business and social elites cultural capital, and firms also show contemporary art on their own premises.
Explains why firms and elites sponsor museums: they gain cultural capital and influence.
Culture Incorporated: Museums, Artists, and Corporate Sponsorships
Corporate sponsorship of museums, artists and cultural events, framed as part of the worldwide privatisation of cultural funding.

Argues corporate sponsorship of artists, museums and events blurs art and public relations. It helps firms keep social legitimacy under criticism, and he calls for full disclosure of corporate involvement.
Explains sponsorship as legitimacy-buying, and the case for publishing sponsor links.
Strategic Responses by a Nonprofit When a Donor Becomes Tainted
Conceptual article on a non-profit that has publicly honoured a donor who then becomes tainted by scandal; no named institution.

Names three outside pressures (clash of values, stakeholders joining forces, visibility) and two inside limits (money need, commitment) that steer an organisation to one of three responses: return the money and drop the honour, keep the money but drop the honour, or keep both.
Gives three outcomes to code for any contested donor: returned, quietly kept, or kept and honoured.
Sponsorship and exhibitions at Nordic science centres and museums
Nordic science centres and science museums; staff accounts of how sponsors affect new exhibitions.

Sponsors are often essential and can shape exhibitions in two ways: openly, by demanding visibility or a say in content, and quietly, as staff trim plans to fit what they think sponsors want, both before and during planning.
Shows sponsor influence can run through self-censorship, so a lack of public conflict is weak proof of independence.
Golfing Alone? Corporations, Elites, and Nonprofit Growth in 100 American Communities
Christopher Marquis; Gerald F. Davis; Mary Ann Glynn, 2013
100 US cities, 1987 to 2002; elite-oriented cultural and educational nonprofits compared with social welfare nonprofits.
More local corporate headquarters meant more new nonprofits of both kinds. Elite-oriented cultural and educational nonprofits gained an extra boost where local elite networks and norms were strong.
Links the local density of firms to the growth of cultural institutions elites sponsor.
Factors of Board Governance and Fundraising Success
Switzerland; regression analysis of board makeup and fundraising across 98 museums.

Museums with donors and business people on their boards did significantly better at fundraising, so board makeup stands out as a driver. The study also discusses organisation size and legal form as further factors.
Direct evidence that seating donors on boards is a fundraising tactic, which supports using shared board seats as a sponsor link.
Artwash: Big Oil and the Arts
Mainly the UK; oil firms (BP, Shell, Chevron, ExxonMobil) and institutions such as Tate and the Southbank Centre, as named by the publisher.

Shows oil firms use arts sponsorship, above all of Tate, to polish their image and screen environmental harm. Draws on undercover research and the Liberate Tate campaign, and notes institutions that dropped oil money.
The core book on artwashing: one industry sponsoring a cluster of national institutions.
Institutional Equivalence: How Industry and Community Peers Influence Corporate Philanthropy
United States; philanthropic contributions by Fortune 1000 firms, 1980 to 2006.
A firm copies most closely the giving of peers that share both its industry and its home city, which the authors call its institutional equivalents.
Explains why companies in the same city and sector end up sponsoring the same institutions.
Opening Spaces of Resistance in the Corporatized Cultural Institution: Liberate Tate and the Art Not Oil Coalition
Britain, mainly Tate; corporate sponsorship of public cultural bodies and the Art Not Oil coalition of artist groups.

With state subsidy worn down, the sector has come to see corporate sponsorship as good. The author critiques how sponsors operate and argues that unauthorised live art inside institutions has begun to break that agreement.
Shows sponsor ties can be contested through sustained action aimed at one institution after subsidy cuts.
Donor governance and financial management in prominent US art museums
Finances of prominent US art museums and gifts that carry donor-set restrictions (summary taken from the 2015 NBER working paper abstract, as the journal abstract could not be read).

Gifts with strings attached have grown and now make up the largest part of museums' permanent capital. Where the strings are tight, spending moves from administration to programmes and savings rise, so such gifts steady a museum but narrow management's freedom.
Shows money can carry control even when the donor is named, so gift conditions are worth noting where known.
Undoing art and oil: an environmental tale of sponsorship, cultural justice and climate change controversy
Britain; the artist collective Liberate Tate and BP's support for the Tate galleries.

The collective recast BP's sponsorship as a governance dispute about market-driven agendas, cultural integrity and climate. Claims of injustice and staged performances unsettled the sponsors' own story, which the author names cultural justice.
Explains how campaigners turn one sponsor tie into a public governance case, the step that usually precedes an exit.
Foundation-funded Journalism, Philanthrocapitalism and Tainted Donors
Kate Wright; Martin Scott; Mel Bunce, 2018
One non-profit news outlet and a donor accused of a large international fraud; this is journalism, not a cultural institution.

Traces how the outlet justified taking the money, what it did to defend its standing and independence, and the conditions under which it finally parted from the foundation. The authors build a model of how non-profits respond to a tainted donor.
Offers a worked example of a funded body defending and then dropping a donor under scandal, to compare with museum cases.
Reducing risky relationships: criteria for forming positive museum-corporate sponsorships
Review of successful and unsuccessful museum-corporate sponsorships (the abstract names no country).
Cuts to public funding for heritage have pushed museums to find corporate partners. The author argues that sponsorships can still help both sides without costing the museum its independence.
Ties falling public money to corporate sponsor links, the condition under which many links on the map arise.
Editorial on university gifts from Epstein, the Sackler family and the Koch brothers, using MIT's Media Lab; it concerns research and education, not culture, and is opinion.

Universities now spend time defending gifts or giving them back. The author says MIT should have stopped its Media Lab taking Epstein's money, blames tight funding and rivalry between institutions, and notes more talk than action.
Frames an Epstein tie as a product of funding pressure, which the atlas can cite for the pattern while noting it covers universities.
Fossil fuel sponsorship and the contested museum
British Museum and BP-sponsored exhibitions, using Freedom of Information requests plus fieldwork on campaigners and on source communities in Australia.

Maps the parties around BP-sponsored shows, from activists to Australian communities, some fighting over returned objects or environmental harm. The authors say attention to these power relations moved the campaign toward arguments rooted in culture.
Shows public-records requests can document a sponsor tie and that campaigns link the museum, the sponsor and affected communities.
America's Cultural Institutions Are Quietly Fueled by Russian Corruption
United States; gifts from seven post-Soviet oligarchs to more than 200 nonprofits, matched from donation records and IRS Form 990 filings.

Seven oligarchs gave an estimated $372 million to $435 million over about two decades to 200-plus nonprofits, including MoMA and the Kennedy Center. The authors call it reputation laundering and report no allegation of illegality.
Shows one donor group reaching many institutions, and the missing donor due-diligence rules.
A.-L. Barabási; A. Grishchenko; A. Gates; L. Shekhtman, 2020
United States; art institutions linked when they share board members, built from nonprofit tax filings.
An interactive map of US art institutions joined by shared board members, drawn from tax forms. The page shows the network and its framing, and gives no statistics.
Closest existing shared-trustee map for US art institutions, built on public tax filings.
Elite philanthropy in the United States and United Kingdom in the new age of inequalities
Mairi Maclean; Charles Harvey; Ruomei Yang; Frank Mueller, 2021
United States and United Kingdom; review of big philanthropy by wealthy individuals, couples and families.

Big giving carries the rich's control from the economy into social and political life. It concentrates power in mega foundations and prestigious charities, and locks in inequality. The review names four types of elite philanthropy.
Frames cultural giving as elite power and offers four types for classifying sponsors.
Patronage as a way out of crisis? the case of major cultural institutions in Spain
Juan Arturo Rubio Aróstegui; Anna Villarroya, 2021
Spain; fifteen flagship cultural institutions in Madrid and Barcelona after the 2008 crisis.

After deep cuts to public culture budgets, direct corporate donations grew in importance for the finances and internal organisation of these state-owned bodies. Who sits on the board is closely tied to how much they raise.
Links public cuts to rising corporate giving and points to the board as where sponsor links form.
Netherlands; three museums funded by Dutch oil and gas firms, studied through interviews, policy papers and analysis of exhibition content.

After 2011-12 reforms pushed cultural entrepreneurship, museums leaned harder on sponsors. The oil and gas money comes with an 'energy literacy' story that suits the industry, and small outlays buy firms large reach in a field the public trusts.
Supports mapping fossil fuel money in Dutch museums and names a policy change as its cause.
'Culture for Sale': The Effects of Corporate Colonization on the UK Museum Sector
Jeremy Aroles; John Stewart Hassard; Paula Hyde, 2021
United Kingdom; interviews with senior museum staff after the 2008 financial crisis and the austerity that followed.

Cuts pushed public museums toward commercial priorities, unevenly: the authors describe three states of exposure, from secure to precarious. Overall, austerity makes museums respond to short-term money needs.
Shows the pull toward private money differs by museum, so exposure to sponsors should not be assumed equal.
"Send Back the Bloodstained Money": Frederick Douglass on Tainted Gifts
Political theory; Douglass's 1846 campaign in Britain against a Scottish church taking slaveholders' gifts, read alongside current calls to return Sackler money.

Douglass held that accepting such gifts bends political relationships and judgement, and he used the campaign to shape public moral reasoning. The author uses this to answer charges of puritanism and hypocrisy against critics of dirty money.
Gives a long-standing argument that taking a donor's money is itself a tie worth recording, with an 1846 precedent for returning it.
Who runs the arts in England? A social network analysis of arts boards
Dave O'Brien; Griffith Rees; Mark Taylor, 2022
England; boards of Arts Council England National Portfolio Organisations, plus the other companies that share their directors.

Most funded arts organisations share no directors with each other. One step out, most are linked indirectly, through film funding and finance companies. The Royal Opera House is the most central node.
Shows how to map shared directors across arts boards using public company records.
Cultural governance within and across cities and regions: Evidence from the English publicly funded arts sector
Dave O'Brien; Griffith Rees; Mark Taylor, 2022
England; boards of Arts Council England National Portfolio Organisations, compared by city and region.

London arts organisations share directors with other companies far more than those elsewhere, and regional ones link mostly to London. London-connected organisations hold over double the funding income.
Shows board sharing concentrates in one city and goes with larger public funding.
'Shell is Proud to Present... The Spirit Sings': Museum Sponsorship and Public Relations in Oil Country
Canada; the 1988 exhibition The Spirit Sings, studied through archives and interviews.

Re-reads a landmark Canadian exhibition through its corporate, national and institutional interests, bringing out the sponsorship and public relations work. Questions whether oil sponsorship debates fit museums in extractive economies.
Historical case tying an oil sponsor to a major museum exhibition.
Bourdieusian capital conversion during crises of socio-political legitimacy: Sponsorship of the arts by Barclays Bank, 1972 to 1987
Ian G. Jones; Nicholas D. Wong; Marta Herrero; Andrew Smith, 2022
Britain; Barclays Bank arts sponsorship, 1972 to 1987.
Barclays raised its arts sponsorship while under attack over apartheid South Africa and high profits, trading economic capital for the prestige of high-status arts institutions.
Documented case of a firm buying cultural prestige to repair its reputation.
Foreign Donations in the Higher Education Sector of the United States and the United Kingdom: Pathways for Reputation Laundering
Alexander Cooley; Tena Prelec; John Heathershaw, 2022
United States and United Kingdom; universities, with a survey of UK development officers (not museums).

Names four routes for laundering reputation through gifts: academic programmes, naming rights, honorary degrees and board seats, plus admissions favours. A survey of UK fundraisers finds legal-compliance checks rarely screen for it.
Lists gift routes, including naming and board seats, that museum donors can be screened against.
Philanthropy in art: locality, donor retention, and prestige
United States; $36 billion in grants from 46,643 foundations to 48,766 art recipients, 2010 to 2019, from IRS e-file data.

Foundation giving to art stays local, with 60% of grants going to recipients in the donor's state. Donors often back several local organisations across artforms, and nearly 70% of funding relationships continue the next year.
Shows one foundation funds many local arts bodies, and gives base rates for donor overlap.
The Interstitial Elites of the Italian Foundations of Banking Origin
Italy; the Compagnia di San Paolo in Turin, one of the foundations of banking origin.
People already powerful elsewhere form a new elite through board seats at a bank-origin foundation. They move between fields as brokers, and use funding and philanthropy to shape public policy.
Case of a funding foundation whose board forms a broker elite across fields.
The art of (self)legitimization: how private museums help their founders claim legitimacy as elite actors
Germany; interviews with founders, directors and curators of private art museums.

Interviewees present private museums as flexible innovators beside public ones, and set the ethical founder-collector against showy collectors and unethical wealth. Founders and their staff both do this legitimation work.
Shows private museums work as status tools, and how insiders defend the founders' standing.
Reputation laundering and museum collections: patterns, priorities, provenance, and hidden crime
Museum antiquities collections; text records of the antiquities trade (the museums' country is not stated in the abstract).

A machine-learning model of antiquities-trade texts flags a decades-long pattern of donating low-value Latin American antiquities to museums to launder reputation, invisible when each museum is checked alone.
Shows donor patterns visible only across museums, the same logic as cross-institution sponsor mapping.
Artistic Activism and Museum Accountability: Staging Antagonism in the Cultural Sphere
United States; the Whitney Museum of American Art and the 2019 protest campaign there.
Examines the 2019 activist campaign at the Whitney, led by Decolonize This Place, which ended with the board vice-chair resigning. Treats the museum as a site of conflict, not neutral ground.
Documents a trustee's resignation after protest, the board-level cost of contested donor links.
Beyond the Global Boom: Private Art Museums in the 21st Century
O. Velthuis; K. Kolbe; J. Aengenheyster; A. Friedmann Rozenbaum; M. Gera; M. Zhang, 2023
Worldwide; database of private museums of modern and contemporary art and their founders.
First systematic overview of private art museums worldwide: founding dates, locations, size and collection focus, founders' gender, age and business backgrounds, and which museums closed and why.
Gives a worldwide list and founder profiles to cross-check against the atlas.
When tainted money should fund public goods: fundraising professional and public moral preferences
US surveys of about 4,600 lay people and 694 professional fundraisers on accepting gifts from morally tainted donors, plus a policy question put to 52 fundraisers.

About half the fundraisers had dealt with a tainted donor, but a policy existed at roughly one institution in three (52 asked). Everyone rejected criminal donors, fundraisers disliked large tainted gifts more, and anonymity barely mattered. Museums and universities faced slightly stricter judgement.
Gives a base rate for how few institutions have a written rule for contested donors.
Who Supports American Art Museums? Introducing a New Dataset and Data Sources about Museum Funding

US; 2019 tax filings of art museums and the foundations that fund them, plus annual reports, centred on fifteen museums of American art (no abstract is published, so this was read from the open article text).

Trustees of these museums rarely sit on more than one board and are mostly local, yet the museums share institutional donors such as the Terra Foundation. Foundation money is lopsided: the Whitney and Crystal Bridges took about $72 million of roughly $110 million in 2019.
Shows that sponsor overlap shows up more in shared funders than in shared trustees, which suits a map built on public filings.
Public art and private wealth: the controversial collaboration between the National Museum in Norway and Fredriksen Family Art Company Ltd
Norway; newspaper coverage of the 2019 ten-year loan deal between the National Museum and a private collector's art company.

The deal drew harsh criticism from the art world once it became public. The authors link the strength of the reaction to Norway's equality norms, trust in paying taxes and long tradition of state support for culture.
Shows a private collector's deal with a public museum works as a sponsor link, and that national funding culture decides how contested it is.
To receive and to give something back - director's perspectives on public - private collaborations in Norwegian art museums
Norway; interviews with eleven directors of publicly funded art museums about working with private collectors.

Directors see public-private collaboration as unavoidable, driven by small purchase budgets, rising costs and fear that public support may shrink as the state leans on oil income. They face criticism and collector demands but stay optimistic.
Shows thin public budgets, not only choice, push public museums toward private collectors.
Case studies of museums' ties to the Sackler family and to the tobacco industry, in a thesis from a US university arts administration programme.

Museums came under heavy pressure to stop taking Sackler money and to strip the family name from buildings, while tobacco money is still taken and rarely questioned. The author argues museums should end tobacco ties and re-examine their gift acceptance policies.
Sets two contested donor industries side by side and marks tobacco as the tie that gets less scrutiny.
The fragility of cultural philanthropy: why private art museums close
Worldwide; a fresh dataset of closed private art museums, analysed with statistics and content analysis.

Closures have several causes and often involve money trouble. Funding models and dependence on one founder make these museums fragile, and at least half of those that closed had been open ten years or less.
Warns that a founder-funded museum on the map may be short-lived and its collection may move on.
Elite Status-Seeking and Class Reproduction in Civil Society: An Analysis of Corporate Elite Appointments to Charity Boards
England and Wales; over 31,000 charity companies, appointments tracked over ten years.
Corporate elites join large, high-status charities, those backing traditional upper-class culture, and grant-giving foundations and think tanks far more than welfare providers.
Shows which kinds of cultural bodies attract corporate elite trustees, and why.
Interviews with museum professionals about how they raise and vet money, set against public backlash over money from harmful industries (the abstract does not name a country).

Argues that everyday fundraising is under-studied and that austerity and market-style museum models make the money choices hard. Wants funding treated as a practice open to ethical debate and reform, with museum staff views counted.
Shows that the route a museum takes to its money, not only the donor's name, belongs on a map of contested funding.
The Dirty Patrons: Environmental Responsibility And Museum Sponsorship
Fossil fuel sponsorship of museums, mainly in Britain, drawn from primary sources; the BP and National Portrait Gallery split is a leading case.

Protests by climate campaigners and artists brought BP's three-decade tie to the National Portrait Gallery to an end in 2022, though the Louvre and the British Museum have kept oil-funded partnerships going. The article stresses trust, openness and financial independence.
Supplies a dated end to a named sponsor tie, plus ties that continue elsewhere, both worth marking on an oil sponsor map.
Beyond Distinction: Private Art Museums and Their Versatile Role for Elites' (Self)Legitimization Discourses
Sara de Andrade Silva; Kristina Kolbe; Olav Velthuis, 2026
399 private art museums in 59 countries; online mission statements analysed by topic modelling.
Private museums present their founders as reliable art-world agents and valuable philanthropists. The arts let wealthy elites from different backgrounds unite globally around private museums.
Shows private museums act as worldwide legitimation tools for wealthy founders.
Modes of Refraction: How Core Museums and Peripheral Art Collectors Co-Produce Cosmopolitan Elite Networks
The Tate and the Centre Pompidou with Hungarian art collectors after 2000, using collection data and interviews.

With public subsidy shrinking, collectors' money is vital to these museums' international collecting. The museums keep acquisition choices inside committees while building a mixed global network of elite patrons that serves collectors' own plans.
Shows a donor network can tie a museum to collectors' private strategies even where decisions look shielded.

title: Small, community-led and state-run institutions
kick: Case study. 13 studies on how small community-led institutions are funded and how state money carries control, each checked against its abstract.
summary: Small community-led institutions run on fragile money. Three London museums showed volatile finances, with donations and grants tied to short-term survival (Bourke and others 2026), and Ontario's community museums lean on spokespeople because they lack resources (Nelson 2020). Control often sits with a larger body. Two Polish museums founded by local campaigns gave communities less say once they opened as city branches (Jagodzińska 2023), an Amsterdam volunteer museum works inside state-led renewal policy (Beeksma and De Cesari 2018), and French funding categories fit hybrid community spaces poorly (Magkou, Pélissier and Pamart 2025). Space matters too: US city cores lost affordable space for studios, galleries and community art centres between two waves of artists' institutional critique (Anagnost 2020). Most of this evidence is single cases, and these institutions remain under-studied (Rey and Schamberger 2026).

Funding is also a channel of control at the top. The UK government steers its national museums by appointing like-minded trustees, through accounting rules, and by stepping in when its aims clash with trustees and curators (Abdullah and Khadaroo 2021). In Denmark subsidy decisions stay with politicians while more of the detail passes to the organisations (Kann-Rasmussen and Rasmussen 2020), and in Italy the autonomy granted to some state museums raised their odds of winning European co-funding (Cavalieri and others 2025). The map counts state money as no flag on its own, and flags it only where the paying state censors or punishes.
On this map, 100 of the 101 institutions still graded Roster unverified are small or mid-sized. Most publish no funder list, or name funders only for single projects.

Records are the other half of the question. The records survey checked the publications of 1002 of the institutions; 996 of those sites could be read, the rest were down or blocked. Of those 996, 415 publish annual reports, 512 publish accounts or statutory filings, 452 name their funders, 578 list their boards, and 288 publish nothing dated about their money. Each institution's panel carries a Records line.
