cells: Participatory heritage in a gentrifying neighbourhood: Amsterdam's Van Eesteren Museum as affective space of negotiations
Amsterdam; the volunteer-built Van Eesteren Museum in the Slotermeer neighbourhood.

Although seen as bottom-up, the museum works as a platform inside Dutch state-led urban renewal and gentrification policy. Volunteers come from a narrow, similar slice of the neighbourhood, while more varied residents stay out.
Shows a community museum can end up serving a city's policy aims, so public backing may tie a small institution to an agenda.
The Museum Community and Community Museum Governance
Ontario, Canada; how museum associations and provincial advisors speak for the 'museum community' across more than 500 museums.

Community museums have little money, so spokespeople speak for them. Municipal museums were historically favoured in associations' picture of the community, while provincial advisors better included small historical society museums. As advisor resources fell, a cash-poor association stepped in and the ranking of museums stayed.
Shows who speaks for small museums in policy depends on larger bodies that are themselves short of resources.
Decentralize! Art, Power, and Space in the New York Art World
New York City art world in the late 1960s to early 1970s and in the 2010s, looking at decentralising institutions as a form of critique.

Two waves of institutional critique are separated by the loss of affordable space for studios, galleries and community art centres in US city cores. The article reads critique as depending on access to space.
Shows rent and space, not only grants, decide whether small and community art venues survive.
Museums lobbied by local communities: potential and actual place of the people in participatory museums of local history
Poland; the Museum of Podgórze in Krakow and the Praga Museum of Warsaw, local-history museums co-created with communities but run as branches of city museums.

Communities were critical in founding both museums, but their role shrank once the doors opened. The museums won standing but gave up room to manoeuvre, and rules and paperwork make taking part harder despite some staff efforts.
Shows a municipal parent institution can absorb a community-founded museum, so who runs the branch matters more than who campaigned for it.
Cause-Based Participative Relationships in Heritage Management
Zagreb, Croatia; the NGO-run Trešnjevka Neighborhood Museum, studied through its website and social media output.

The museum is managed jointly by NGOs, museum institution representatives and residents. It forms a community of interest around heritage values that differ from mainstream institutions, and its governance mixes corporatist and service-led features. The abstract does not discuss funding.
Shows a neighbourhood museum shares control among several partners, so a funding map should treat it as a network and not a single owner.
The 'tiers-lieux culturels' as cultural and social infrastructures, and their support in French public policies
Matina Magkou; Maud Pélissier; Émilie Pamart, 2025
France; cultural third places in southern France, studied through policy documents, interviews with founders and managers, and observation.

Policies for these hybrid spaces strain against funding frameworks that do not fit their mixed identities. The strain comes from clashes between market-minded creative-city ideas and cultural-rights, participatory ideas, and from policymakers' hopes for them.
Shows public funding categories can misfit hybrid community spaces, leaving them with money on terms that do not match what they do.
Culture-specific libraries, archives and museums: beyond regimes of factuality
Australia; forum introduction on community-led libraries, archives and museums run by migrant, diaspora and other culture-based communities since the 1950s.

These bodies sit apart from the main state institutions, act as sites of cultural labour, and have uneasy dealings with state institutions and funding bodies. The authors call them under-studied; the piece reports no funding figures.
Confirms a data gap: small community-led institutions are poorly documented, so a map must lean on case sources.
Practicing Strategic Financial Sustainability in Small Cultural Non-Profits: Evidence From London Museums
Joseph Gerald Bourke; Albert Amanollahnejad; Javad Izadi Z.D.; Dinusha Weerawardane, 2026
London; three small museums, using six years of audited accounts and interviews with trustees and senior managers.

Finances stay volatile, with donations and grants linked to short-term viability. Survival depends on constant adaptation and winning legitimacy, and reporting and governance routines serve partly as a display that wins resources while the weakness stays out of sight.
Shows small museums lean on donations and grants and report in ways that can mask weakness, which supports calls for flexible funding.
Reframing entrepreneurship: an upside-down pyramid perspective on community-led social and cultural sustainability
Giusy Sica; Chiara Spiniello; Maria Palazzo; Giovanna Lusini, 2026
Southern Italy; Officina Keller, a community-oriented cultural enterprise, studied through 15 stakeholder interviews alongside a review of 1,155 articles.

Community cohesion, local revival and cultural memory drive the enterprise, but thin institutional and technical backing persists. The authors call for policy that better fits the social and cultural aims of place-based community projects.
Adds a case of a community-led cultural enterprise with thin public backing, to set beside sponsor-funded flagship institutions.
Case Studies in Advancing Community Priorities Through Museum-Community Participatory Science Partnerships
Marcos Aguilar; Aretzy Amaya; Ary Amaya; Melissa Ballard, 2026
Three museum-community partnerships (bird flu, food access and climate, Indigenous youth conservation) told by the co-authors, with formal evaluation; the abstract names no museum or country.

Lessons include that shared leadership takes deliberate effort and trust, that project scope must match resources, and that funders who are flexible and trusting are essential. It rests on the project teams' own experience.
Names trust-based philanthropy as a condition for co-created community work, though the evidence is the authors' own projects.

Paradoxical autonomy in cultural organisations: an analysis of changing relations between cultural organisations and their institutional environment, with examples from libraries, archives and museums
Review of public administration research applied to libraries, archives and museums; no single country is named in the abstract.

Cultural organisations face more focus on social value, users and performance measures, which cuts autonomy, yet gain room to find new ways of meeting their purpose. Subsidy decisions stay with politicians, while more of the policy detail passes to the organisations themselves.
Cautions against reading funder control as simply rising or falling, since funding conditions shift roles without removing discretion.
Controlling UK national museums and galleries: the pursuit of conflicting politico-economic and socio-cultural objectives
United Kingdom; national museums and galleries in London, from published sources and interviews with sponsors, trustees and senior managers.

Government steers these museums by appointing like-minded trustees, through accounting controls and by stepping in directly when its aims clash with trustees and curators. As funding falls and self-earned income is urged, museums ask for more say over spending.
Shows state money and trustee appointments are control channels, so board links on the map should include state appointees.
Do governance features shape museum behaviour? Insights from participation to competitive funding
Marina Cavalieri; Antonio Gallea; Marco Ferdinando Martorana; Ilde Rizzo, 2025
Italy; museums and similar institutions, tracking who enters and wins European competitive funding calls, with a staggered difference-in-differences test of special autonomy.
A museum's internal makeup and its governance status, such as special autonomy, both raise its odds of joining European co-funded projects. The boost from autonomy strengthens over time.
Shows a state's choice of governance model affects which museums can reach competitive public money.

title: Who publishes what about their money
kick: Case study. What 1,013 institutions publish about their own money, by grade and by country, from the records survey and filed accounts.
summary: This study counts what each institution publishes about its own money: annual reports, accounts or statutory filings, a list of funders, and its board. The records survey covered 1,013 institutions on the map; 1,007 of their sites could be read, the rest were down or blocked.

Of the 1,007 readable sites, 460 publish no accounts of any kind, and 371 show no funders at all; another 157 show sponsors only as logos, with no names. 415 publish annual reports and 578 list their boards. 314 publish nothing dated about their money: no report, no accounts and no named funder.

Openness does not follow the grade. 184 of the 348 flagged institutions name their funders, against 150 of the 376 Verified ones. Most flags come from funders the institutions name themselves, so an institution that names no one is harder to grade.

Filed accounts give income figures for 410 institutions; 351 of them show the public share, and 138 take half or more of their income from public bodies. The country table gives the median public share where at least one filing shows it.

title: What the field says: e-flux, BAK, The Otolith Group and artists' own texts
kick: Case study. 68 essays, letters, films, books and statements on how art institutions are funded and governed, read at e-flux, BAK, The Otolith Group, two groups of artists, a Berlin book launch and the texts on Tanja Ostojić, each paraphrased in the editor's words and linked to its source.
summary: e-flux is where much of this argument has been made, and where this map's list of institutions began. Its journal has argued since 2015 that art runs on finance, tax havens and insider networks (Steyerl, 2015 and 2016); that oil sponsorship buys legitimacy, and that the campaigns against it at Tate, the Louvre and the British Museum form one movement (Demos, 2017); and that museums absorb critique, so the 2019 protest at the Whitney over Warren Kanders both wounded and fed the institution (Petrossiants, 2020). Writers have named the money behind MoMA's board (Heddaya and Sahakian, 2020; Ramadan, 2020; Gómez-Barris, 2023), traced art strikes from Sydney and São Paulo to Abu Dhabi (Öğüt, 2015; Szreder, 2017), and read the 2026 Venice Biennale strike and the Qatar Museums pavilion gift as a crisis of its governance (Majaca, 2026; Art Not Genocide Alliance, 2026). e-flux also carries the open letters: on Kunsthalle Berlin's public subsidies (2022), museum education workers (2020), Berlin's funding clause (2024), documenta fifteen (2022) and the Whitney's Independent Study Program (2025). e-flux does not say how it is funded; institutions, some on this map, pay for its announcements.

BAK speaks from inside the question. Its authors argue for instituting otherwise: running an art institution as public practice rather than a venue, and paying for work through cooperatives rather than grants (Hlavajova and van Heeswijk, 2019; van Heeswijk, 2019). Hlavajova called the Venice Biennale a neoliberal model as early as 2011. In 2024 Utrecht ended BAK's multi-year subsidy and the Council for Culture advised ending state funding; BAK says the city's own advisory report had praised it and calls the cut a deliberate weakening of critical organisations (BAK, 2024). Lütticken puts the lost money at almost half its budget, and four post-academic institutions wrote in support. BAK now runs as a defunded Basecamp (2025). Lütticken also faults the Stedelijk's reliance on big donors and its silence on Gaza (e-flux journal, 2025). The lesson for the map is that the state is both funder and the party that can withdraw.

The Otolith Group reads today's finance through its colonial origins. Kodwo Eshun and Anjalika Sagar, drawing on Ian Baucom, trace a market built on marine insurance and credit back to the slave trade, and read the 1781 Zong case, in which owners claimed insurance for drowned captives, as a logic of economic necessity that traders and insurers still share (LUX interview, 2010; Cox, 2014). Hydra Decapita (2010) stages that argument as an allegory of finance capital, and INFINITY minus Infinity (2019) joins the unpaid debts of racial capitalism to climate catastrophe. Their 2017 programme Climates of Fiction names corporate extraction as the cause of the climate crisis and screens BP's mid-century photographs of Iran. The 2023 Otolith Manifesto refuses the demands institutions make for accountability, recognisability and representability, and names no funder. For this map, the point is that the money behind institutions has a history, and insurance and extraction are part of it.

The artists of The People's Art, Bartomeu Marí's farewell show at Witte de With (now Kunstinstituut Melly) in 2001 to 2002, answered the Dutch consensus society with images of disorder; few of them have addressed how institutions are paid for. Aernout Mik's Middlemen (2001) stages a trading floor of nervous dealers, and Julika Rudelius's Economic Primacy (2005) and Rituals (2012) record how money speaks through lawyers, executives and the gestures of global capitalism. Nasrin Tabatabai and Babak Afrassiabi's Seep (2012) sets a British Petroleum oil archive beside the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art's Western collection, assembled in the 1970s oil boom and stored in cellars after 1979. No boycott, open letter or dispute with an institution on the map was found for any of the fifteen.

Among artists shown at De Appel since 2022, the record is about the institutions around them. In 2024 thirteen signatories, including Alina Lupu, Raul Balai and Pieter Paul Pothoven, said the Stedelijk refused to lend Ahmet Öğüt's Bakunin's Barricade to protect protesting students (Not Surprised, 2024; Lupu, 2024). De Appel's own history carries the 2015 dispute, when its board dismissed director Lorenzo Benedetti, the Curatorial Programme tutors asked the board to resign (Exibart, 2015), and a city inquiry found the board fell short (Knight, 2015). In 2024 the Amsterdam Fund for the Arts first planned to cut De Appel's award to a quarter of the advised sum before a coalition of institutions won the full amount (De Appel, 2025), and the city's institutions now ask for 4.4 million euros more a year (MOKER, 2026).

The newest entry is Luïza Luz's book and launch at soft power, a collectively run non-profit art space in a former factory in Berlin-Tempelhof, on 23 October 2026. The spread shown in the listing is headed In Defiance, We Listen Deeper. Its right-hand column is cut off in the listing's image, so only part of the argument is legible: the surface gives a partial first impression, and a way of knowing led by sight and intellect favours what can be seen and measured. The book names no institution or funder. Luz's earlier book, Beneath the Surface (Archive Books and we make it, 2024), examines academic institutions that repeat selective stories. Her 5 November 2025 lecture at kex Vienna sat in an exhibition funded by DGARTES, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation and the Mondriaan Fund. No page was found for a book titled In Defiance, We Listen Deeper, so it is unclear whether it is a new title or a new edition of Beneath the Surface.

Tanja Ostojić's work is about who holds power in art institutions, and the texts about her say little on money. Her own 2016 statement says the Q21 show in Vienna's MuseumsQuartier cut her budget and publicity before she withdrew, an account Hyperallergic reported as an allegation. In a 2017 interview, published in 2019, she says German funding, including the Goethe-Institut Belgrade, let her show in former Yugoslav museums, and that citizenship decides who gets funded. Bojana Videkanić (2009) and Anna Mikaela Ekstrand (2026) read her curator projects, including shadowing Harald Szeemann at the 2001 Venice Biennale, as critique of curatorial power. Her own introduction to the 2004 book Strategies of Success / Curators Series says the project was shown in full only once, at La BOX in Bourges in 2003, and that it analyses class relations and power in the art system. None of these texts criticises an institution on the map, so none adds a line to a pin.

cells: 1 year of BAK Basecamp: we are alive, kicking and here to stay!
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

The collective says Utrecht ended BAK's multi-year subsidy and the Council for Culture followed, leaving BAK fully defunded. Basecamp began in 2025 on friction money and BAK's reserve, flattened its labour fees, runs on a sociocratic model and lists seven funders.
It names the private funds that now carry BAK next to the municipality and shows a defunded institution moving to foundation money and flatter pay.
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

Lütticken says BAK's propositions programme grew from working inside neoliberalised Dutch funding, and faults it for never defining a proposition. He says the Stedelijk Museum relies on high-profile donors and has not answered Gaza in its programme, and he wants documenta's terms of success challenged.
Stedelijk Museum, BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, documenta
A named critic links BAK's loss of public money and the Stedelijk's donor dependence to what he calls a wider defunding and criminalisation of dissent, and to boycott calls such as Strike Germany.
NO BUSINESS AS USUAL: Culturele Boycot van Israël
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

The post reports a campaign by Dutch and Belgian artists and cultural institutions to end cooperation with Israeli state bodies, institutions and firms. The campaign frames this as aimed at institutional complicity in breaches of international law, not individuals, and exempts organisations opposing the occupation.
It adds a cultural boycott call carried on BAK Basecamp's blog; the page lists BAK's funders but does not state whether BAK itself signed.
BAK announces Basecamp for Tactical Imaginaries: Building Cultural Infrastructure Anew
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

Team BAK says Utrecht's city government dropped its multi-year subsidy and the national Council for Culture advised ending state funding, though the city's advisory report praised BAK's practice. BAK calls this one modest case of deliberate weakening of critical organisations and answers with Basecamp.
Municipality of Utrecht, Raad voor Cultuur
BAK cites a fall in the visual-art share of Utrecht's 2025 to 2028 culture budget from 6.7% to 1.61%, and still lists the city among its Basecamp supporters.
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

Lütticken reports that Utrecht's municipality is withdrawing funding worth almost half of BAK's budget and says the decision, if it stands, ends vital infrastructure. He argues that progressive city councils in effect do the far right's work, and points to BAK's own statement.
A BAK collaborator puts the municipal share of BAK's budget at almost 50%, the clearest published figure for how dependent BAK was on one public funder.
Responses to our Solidarity Call Out
De Ateliers; EKWC; Jan van Eyck Academie; Rijksakademie, 2024
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

After the committee advised defunding BAK, peers, a cleaners' union and academics wrote to the city. Four post-academic schools say BAK is one of five such institutions in the national basic infrastructure, backing about 150 artists yearly, and that cutting it endangers the ecosystem.
It shows who stood with BAK when the Utrecht advice came, from peer institutions on the same national funding line to a labour union and university staff.
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

BAK stands with ruangrupa, the artists and the lumbung ecosystem at documenta fifteen. It quotes Sami Khatib calling the antisemitism accusations a fruitless attempt to discipline ruangrupa, and it describes the German debate as part of racist and imperial politics.
It records one institution defending another in a dispute over state and press pressure on a major exhibition, though the statement says nothing about documenta's funding.
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

The editors treat today's culture wars as ground chosen by the right, where fighting means losing, and propose tactical desertion instead of reactive replies. John Beeson's review reads the book as favouring economic solidarity over culture-war politics.
It gives the culture-war framing used by BAK's research programme; Beeson's review ties the term to US fights over defunding the National Endowment for the Arts.
Maria Hlavajova; Jeanne van Heeswijk; Andrea Philips; Laura Raicovich, 2019
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

The BAK symposium says Western art institutions, in ways that echo colonial habits, depoliticise art by claiming neutrality, and proposes instituting otherwise: running every process with the communities served. A workshop for institutions, funds and policy makers was timed to the Dutch four-year funding round.
Its announcement names the ministry, the city and several funds, and shows BAK pitching institutional reform to funders and policy makers inside the funding cycle that later cut it.
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

Van Heeswijk says art spaces carry colonial legacies yet stay civic spaces for hard conversations. She favours cooperative businesses that sustain projects without grants, citing Homebaked in Liverpool, and separates participation inside a frame from co-creation that questions the frame.
A BAK fellow describes a funding route of cooperative trading plus non-art public money, and names the Liverpool Biennial as the commissioner of Homebaked.
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

Lütticken argues that autonomy is an act, not a possession, since institutional critique accepted that nothing lies outside art's institutions. He reads Hans Haacke's The Chase Advantage as showing sponsorship polishing a bank's image, and says the culturalisation of labour ties art to the economy.
A BAK-linked author gives a short theoretical account of sponsorship as image work for a bank, without figures or institutions on the map.
Call the Witness: An Interview with Maria Hlavajova
BAK, basis voor actuele kunst, Utrecht

Hlavajova describes the Venice Biennale as a neoliberal model tied to national representation and the market, where critical projects get absorbed. She presents the Roma Pavilion, supported by Open Society Foundations, as an attempt to work outside both the market and the nation-state.
It shows a private foundation backing a Venice pavilion for a group without a national patron, with the curator's own critique of the Biennale's market logic.
Luïza Luz (soft power, Berlin; Archive Books)

In the legible part of the spread, Luz says the surface gives only a partial first impression and invites conclusions assumed rather than felt. She ties a way of knowing led by sight and intellect, shaped by long traditions, to narratives of the visible.
It names no institution or funder; it adds an artist's argument that trusting what can be seen and measured narrows the stories institutions tell.
Beneath the Surface: Deep Listening, Buried Narratives, and Embodied Resistance
Luïza Luz (soft power, Berlin; Archive Books)

Luz presents embodied resistance as a way to make knowledge and treats deep listening as theory and practice. Drawing on a year of writing, the book examines academic institutions that keep repeating a chosen set of stories, and argues for turning trauma into ecological liberation.

The 2025 lecture at kex Vienna, where Luz presented this work, sat in an exhibition funded by DGARTES, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation and the Mondriaan Fund, so the platforms for this critique can be traced.

The group says it refuses the demands institutions place on it for accountability, recognisability and representability. It ties those demands to numbers and statistics and to institutions organised by area-studies categories, and describes itself as an interscalar vehicle that does not fit that format.
A statement from a collective that Ibraaz lists as publicly funded by Arts Council England, on how institutions measure and sort artists; it names no funder, institution or boycott.

A 51-minute film that joins the unpaid debts of racial capitalism to climate catastrophe as one history. It stages the UK hostile environment policy against the Windrush generation, drawing on Una Marson, Glissant, Denise Ferreira da Silva, Saidiya Hartman, Christina Sharpe and Kathryn Yusoff.

The group's credits list the Sharjah Architecture Triennial (SAT01) as commissioner and Z33 as co-producer, with support from ICA London, so a critique of racial capitalism has named public and Gulf commissioners.
Climates of Fiction: Cinemas from the Capitalocene

The group's curatorial text reads the present as a geological age shaped by corporate extraction, which it names the Capitalocene. The film programme covers oil, nuclear power, settler colonialism and slavery tied to mineral extraction, including a film on BP's photographs of mid-century Iran.
A curatorial statement from the group that names corporate extraction as the cause of the climate crisis and puts BP's colonial-era archive on screen, at an independent London venue.
Afrofuturism, Afro-Pessimism and the Politics of Abstraction: A Conversation with Kodwo Eshun

Eshun says the group used the Drexciya myth to read the 2008 financial crisis. Citing Ian Baucom, he says the slave trade started a world market built on insurance and credit, and that the Zong case was a fight over insurance, not murder.
Shows a member of the group tying a film about slavery to the 2008 crisis and to marine insurance, which frames colonial capital as the root of financial abstraction.
What form would that abstraction take now? The Otolith Group in Conversation with Gil Leung (Part 2 of 3)
Kodwo Eshun; Anjalika Sagar; Gil Leung, 2010

Eshun and Sagar, citing Ian Baucom, say marine insurance, bills of exchange and the slave trade formed an early finance market. They read the Zong case as a language of economic necessity shared by traders and insurers that persists today.
Gives the group's own account of slave-trade insurance and credit as the origin of finance, a source for any record that ties institutional money to colonial-era capital.

A 31-minute video installation that starts from Drexciya's underwater myth and the 1781 Zong killings, where the owners claimed insurance for drowned captives. The group's page calls it a “séance on capitalism and slavery”; MACBA's entry reads it as an allegory of finance capital.
Records that the Manifesta Foundation commissioned the film for Manifesta 8 and that MACBA acquired it in 2012, so a work on insurance money sits in a public museum collection.
artists of The People's Art (Witte de With, Rotterdam)

The e-flux announcement says Mik's multichannel video sets new religious communities beside secular business gatherings, and says such movements follow the model of international companies while promising material prosperity along with redemption.
It links corporate organisation to belief and promised wealth; no institution is named.
artists of The People's Art (Witte de With, Rotterdam)

The announcement on e-flux says Tabatabai and Afrassiabi set a British Petroleum archive of Iranian oil operations beside the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art's Western collection, assembled in the 1970s oil boom and stored in cellars after 1979, and treat both as suspended archives.
It ties the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art's Western collection to the 1970s oil boom and to its removal from view after 1979, as the artists present it.
artists of The People's Art (Witte de With, Rotterdam)

Leo Koenig Inc.'s press release says Rudelius's film Rituals, begun on a 2010 residency in Guangzhou, studies gestures drawn from global capitalism: young men posing in traffic, a street magician multiplying a coin, men throwing banknotes at working-class women.
It is an artist's study of how wealth is performed in public; the release names no institution or funder.
artists of The People's Art (Witte de With, Rotterdam)
The Videoart at Midnight listing on reinhardhauff.de says Rudelius filmed five men, among them a lawyer, a millionaire and a senior executive, speaking about how important and all-reaching money is.
It records how wealthy professionals talk about money, as the listing describes it; no institution or arts funder is named.
artists of The People's Art (Witte de With, Rotterdam)
MoMA's 2009 press release says Mik's Middlemen shows a stock market floor or commodities exchange where workers wait nervously for something unknown, with a camera that moves as jitterily as they do.
The Witte de With page for The People's Art illustrates the show with a still from this work, and it takes a financial market as its scene; the release names no institution as a target.
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

MOKER, the network of Amsterdam visual arts institutions, says the sector is under heavy pressure. Zone2Source's summary says it asks for 4.4 million euros more a year and policy changes from the City, the Arts Council and the Arts Fund, with Stedelijk support.
A 2026 sector-wide funding demand backed by the Stedelijk Museum; per De Appel's 2022 report, its then business director founded MOKER in 2019.
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

De Appel's own report says the Amsterdam Fund for the Arts first planned to cut its 2025 to 2028 award to 25 percent of the advised amount. A coalition of institutions below the funding line then won the full sum, with alderwoman Touria Meliani's help.
It is a first-hand account of a municipal funding shortfall settled by lobbying, alongside a full Mondriaan Fonds award of 450,000 euros a year.
Every Act of Struggle: Intrusion and Assembly
School of Intrusions; Noor Abed; Chad Cordeiro; Pieter Paul Pothoven, 2025
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

De Appel's page says the show sets the Dutch anti-apartheid cultural boycott and artist actions beside today's pressure on institutions to face colonial history, notes that many institutions respond privately and cautiously, and asks whether present tools of resistance are enough.
It links a historic cultural boycott to current institutional silence; the page lists Het Cultuurfonds as the only funder.
Jack Segbars; Pascal Gielen; Koen Bartijn; Sepp Eckenhaussen, 2025
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

De Appel's report says the first day asked how to read the defunding of institutions, how neoliberal ideology shapes arts subsidies and how to move beyond dependence on the state; the second day explored community currencies independent of banks.
A programme on cuts to cultural budgets, hosted at De Appel on 16 and 17 May 2025, the year its own four-year funding began.
Stedelijk Museum Fails to Loan Artwork by Ahmet Ögüt to Protect Students in Amsterdam
Not Surprised Collective; Alina Lupu; Pieter Paul Pothoven; Raul Balai, 2024
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

Thirteen signatories say the Stedelijk refused their 28 May 2024 request to lend Ahmet Ögüt's Bakunin's Barricade to protect protesting students, offered replicas and a talk instead, and put its own interests ahead of human rights.
It gives a dated, named case of a museum declining a protest-related loan, which a funding map can set beside the Stedelijk's municipal and corporate backers.
How the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam refused to let ‘Bakunin’s Barricade’ be an actual barricade against the ongoing genocide
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

Lupu says the Stedelijk offered replicas or indoor display instead of a loan. She reports director Rein Wolfs telling a 9 November 2024 panel that the museum makes no political statements, and argues this contradicts its earlier statements on Ukraine and Black Lives Matter.
It adds a named director's stated position on museum neutrality, relevant to how a museum with municipal and corporate backers answers political demands.
Collective Study in Times of Emergency. A Roundtable
Nick Aikens; Sara Buraya Boned; Charles Esche; Ovidiu Ţichindeleanu, 2024
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

Esche says the state in Western Europe is turning disciplinary and that L'Internationale's member organisations are funded by and complicit with the EU and states. Other speakers describe censorship of pro-Palestine voices and EU funding that preserves the status quo.
Esche, a De Appel Curatorial Programme tutor in 2015, ties museum funding by the EU and states to complicity, a frame a funding map can apply to L'Internationale's member museums.
‘I am not an anti-Semite’: Pro-Palestine artists cancelled across Europe
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

Al Jazeera reports that Alsharif withdrew from IDFA in November 2023 after organisers condemned a pro-Palestine protest at the opening. She calls the antisemitism charge a tactic used against Palestinians and a dangerous precedent for punishing personal political views.
A named artist's withdrawal from an Amsterdam festival over its response to protest; IDFA is not on the map, and Alsharif had a solo show at De Appel in 2024.
Right now, today, we must say that Palestine is the centre of the world
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

Vergès says the City of Paris had a public meeting with Judith Butler cancelled and threatened to cut subsidies, and that other venues declined the event for fear of losing funding. She calls this censorship and faults cultural bodies for bans and disinvitations.
A named case of a city threatening subsidies to stop an event, from a speaker at De Appel's May 2025 L'Internationale programme.
Permanent Tijdelijk: over innovatie in de kunst en de behoefte aan continuïteit
Ann Demeester; Araf Ahmadali; Marjo van Schaik; Eelco van der Lingen, 2022
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

De Appel's report says the round table asked what duties a retreating municipal and national government has toward art in Amsterdam, and what a diverse staff means when wages must stay low, and that venues are hollowed out when left to local and national policy.
A 2022 De Appel round table on precarity, short leases and low pay in a subsidised centre, in the institution's own words.
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

De Craen reads the board's 14 September 2015 dismissal of director Lorenzo Benedetti as a sign of managerial culture in the arts. She notes no visual artist sits on De Appel's board and says funding now turns on figures, citing a Mondriaan Fund application.
It is a named, same-month critique of who sits on De Appel's board and of funding rules that push boards toward managers.
Lorenzo Benedetti deve lasciare definitivamente il De Appel. A deciderlo è La Corte del distretto di Amsterdam. Posizione che solleva una questione cruciale nel mondo dell'arte
Charles Esche; Elena Filipovic; Chus Martinez; Beatrix Ruf, 2015
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

Exibart reports on 4 December 2015 that the Curatorial Programme tutors, among them Esche, Filipovic, Martinez and Ruf, backed Benedetti, asked De Appel's board to resign and withdrew from the programme until it was renewed. Exibart gives no signatory count.
It shows the programme's own teachers, per Exibart, demanding the resignation of the board that dismissed the director.
De Appel: Advies commissie Swaab in tegenspraak met advies Raad voor Cultuur
artists shown at De Appel, Amsterdam

Knight reports that the Swaab commission, set up by Amsterdam, found De Appel's board fell short through an informal culture without clear agreements or a job description, yet accepted its decision to start dismissal. He argues this contradicts the Raad voor Cultuur's 2012 praise.
It records, per Knight, an independent municipal finding dated 3 December 2015 on how the board of a centre receiving a 500,000 euro subsidy was run.
On the Making of the May 8 Strike at the 61st Venice Biennale

The Alliance describes a 24-hour walkout by cultural workers, joined by Italian unions, in support of Palestine and workers' rights. It argues that the Biennale's governance and funding push political risk onto precarious artists and staff, enable artwashing and depend on underpaid workers.
It is a first-hand organiser account of a labour strike at a major biennale and of what the organisers say about its funding and staffing.
What Did the Golden Lion Die Of? On Judgment and Disavowal at the Venice Biennale

Majaca argues that when the 2026 jury excluded states whose leaders face International Criminal Court charges, La Biennale replaced the prize with a public vote. She links its Mussolini-era concession structure and a Qatar Museums donation for a pavilion to a spread of responsibility.
It connects a state donor's pavilion concession (Majaca cites a 50 million euro gift tied to 90 years) to the Biennale's governance, material for the Venice Biennale entry.

Heiser argues that Gulf states treat art, like sport and tourism, as an investment to diversify oil-dependent economies, and that this goes beyond artwashing. Culture becomes a tool of geopolitical brokerage and elite networking, which he calls "cartographic cynicism".
It places an art fair and Western institutions' Gulf projects inside a state investment strategy in Qatar and the UAE, which bears on how the map should read Gulf-backed institutions.
The Fifth Estate: On Museums, Public Imagination, and the Vanishing Space for Collectivity (A Report from Flanders, Belgium), Part 2

Pirotte and Silvrants-Barclay argue that Flanders lets private actors such as the Phoebus Foundation and Katoen Natie gain prestige and indirect state aid while public museums face cuts. They compare French and UK tax-incentive regimes and call for safeguards against donor influence.
It explains how tax relief rules and state goodwill let private foundations and collectors gain public standing, a mechanism for reading mixed private and public museums.
Thinking Infrastructurally: On Diversity of Aesthetics, Part 1

Kukuljevic argues that the museum-gallery-biennial system absorbs institutional critique and keeps its moral authority intact, and proposes treating institutions as resources to rearrange. In a Strike MoMA roundtable, former MoMA educator Shellyne Rodriguez says she was fired for urging staff to unionise.
It reports a former employee's account of dismissal for organising and ties MoMA's freelance education staffing to the critique of institutions.
To the Whitney Museum of American Art
Whitney Independent Study Program alumni, faculty and friends, 2025

Over 200 alumni, faculty and friends of the Whitney's Independent Study Program back its 2024 to 2025 cohort, whose Palestine work they say the museum censored. They oppose a cancelled performance and criticise what they call the board's financial ties to genocide in Gaza.
A 2025 case of signatories linking a museum's censorship decision to its board's financial interests; the letter names no individual trustees or funders.
Disinheriting the Violence of Colonial Modernity: Art, Exhibition-Making, and Infra/Intra-structural Critique

Abudu argues that art institutions under racial capitalism are materially bound to colonial wealth through funders, collectors and markets, so decolonial gestures get absorbed. Using Cameron Rowland's mortgage of the ICA London's mahogany fittings, the essay says change means confronting financial dependencies.
It argues the financial dependencies of exhibition-making, not only exhibition content, carry colonial money, which supports flagging funder type for institutions.
Open Letter to the Berlin Senate Cultural Administration and to Joe Chialo, State Minister for Culture and Social Cohesion

More than 2,000 Berlin cultural workers demand the Senate withdraw a clause making acceptance of the IHRA definition of antisemitism a condition of cultural funding. They argue it threatens artistic freedom, enables cancellations of critics of Israel and fosters self-censorship.
It documents a state funder attaching a political condition to arts grants, a form of state control over funded institutions and artists.

Gómez-Barris argues that museums and collections are funded by oil, mining, weapons and media fortunes whose violence the institutions hide. She names the Rockefeller, Getty, Guggenheim and Cisneros families and Warren Kanders, and calls for exposure, restitution and redirected resources.
It links named donor families' extractive wealth to MoMA and the Whitney, a historical argument for tracing money back to oil, mining and weapons.
Open Letter: Who Owns the Public?
Jörg Heiser; Hito Steyerl; Clemens von Wedemeyer, 2022

Heiser, Steyerl and von Wedemeyer say Berlin officials let a private network use public land, a lease and subsidies for Kunsthalle Berlin, and that this launders its sponsors' reputations. They demand the lease end, the Tempelhof agreement be published, and ethics rules for public-private ties.
It documents, in the signatories' account, a publicly subsidised venue tied to private sponsors including energy, arms and data firms, a pattern a funding map should be able to flag.

Thomas argues that Documenta 15 puts Global South collectives in a double bind: funding builds infrastructure yet often serves donors' political interests. She reports an investigation into whether one group's inclusion breached a 2019 Bundestag anti-BDS resolution, after which it left Kassel.
It sets donor influence and a federal parliament's resolution side by side as pressures on a state-funded exhibition.
Censorship Must Be Refused: Letter from lumbung community

Artists and collectives of documenta fifteen reject their supervisory board's call to have scholars review the artworks for antisemitism, calling it censorship that breeds self-censorship. They also demand action on harassment, racism and attacks on participants.
A primary statement from artists to the board of documenta about oversight and censorship, though it names no funders.

Heddaya and Sahakian review MoMA PS1's Gulf Wars show and say it avoids its own funders, above all MoMA board chair Leon Black, whose firm Apollo owned contractors that became Constellis. They call "toxic philanthropy" an imprecise label that treats the donor's identity as fixable.
It ties a named board chair's private-equity holdings to the Iraq war and argues that donor money is built into how art is funded, which supports tracing trustees' business interests on the map.
Inside and Out: The Edges to Critique

Petrossiants argues that museums absorb critical gestures and turn them into performance, so artists who enter or leave an institution often strengthen it. Drawing on the 2019 campaign against Whitney vice chair Warren Kanders, he calls for collective, abolitionist struggle beyond inside and outside.
It places the 2019 Kanders campaign in a longer history of artists acting against museum boards, useful for tracing which boards drew protest.
Theater of Operations: The Gulf Wars 1991–2011

Ramadan reviews the MoMA PS1 exhibition and says MoMA and PS1 are tied to military and prison industries through trustees with investments in private prisons and ICE detention. She reports that Phil Collins withdrew his work and Michael Rakowitz paused his video in protest.
It records artist withdrawals aimed at named trustees' investments and, in the reviewer's account, the museum's refusal to cut ties.
Open letter to museums and galleries in support of education and other essential workers
Academics, curators, artists and educators (100 signatories), 2020

Signatories criticise museums for cutting freelance and part-time education staff during COVID-19, naming MoMA, MOCA Los Angeles, MASS MoCA and the Serralves Foundation. They demand reversed layoffs and secure, fairly paid contracts for all cultural workers.
MoMA, MOCA Los Angeles, MASS MoCA, Serralves Foundation
It shows which large institutions the signatories say shed precarious educators in 2020, adding a labour dimension to the funding picture.
Forensic Architecture; Praxis Films; Laura Poitras, 2019

Forensic Architecture and Praxis Films trained computer vision to find Safariland's Triple-Chaser tear gas canisters in online images, using a digital model in synthetic scenes. The page identifies Safariland's owner, Warren Kanders, as Whitney vice chair; the Whitney invited the project to its 2019 Biennial.
It is the work through which a trustee's weapons business was examined, and it fed the 2019 campaign that preceded his July 2019 resignation from the Whitney board.

Dimitrakaki argues that museums' acceptance of Sackler money tied to opioid profits turns radical feminism into reform that serves the museum's self-legitimation, and that liberal critics blamed marketing rather than capitalism. She cites the 2018 protest at the Met and Tate's BP sponsorship.
One of few e-flux texts found that treats Sackler gifts at the Met as a funding problem, though it is one section of a wider essay.

cells: Accumulation (from The Great Transition: The Arts and Radical System Change)

Demos argues that oil and gas sponsorship (BP, Total, Eni, Shell) buys cultural institutions public legitimacy and makes them complicit in climate harm. He treats Liberate Tate, BP or Not BP and allied campaigns as a movement that makes museums sites of political action.
Tate Modern, Tate Britain, Louvre, American Museum of Natural History, British Museum
It sets named fossil-fuel sponsors against named museums and the campaigns that opposed them, a documented basis for flagging oil money on the map.
Productive Withdrawals: Art Strikes, Art Worlds, and Art as a Practice of Freedom

Szreder argues that art strikes, boycotts and occupations are productive withdrawals that generate collective creativity and new commons-based institutions. He surveys the 2014 boycotts of Manifesta, the São Paulo and Sydney biennials, Poland's art workers' strike and Gulf Labor actions at the Guggenheim.
Biennale of Sydney, Fundação Bienal de São Paulo, Guggenheim Abu Dhabi
A survey of art-world boycotts and strikes up to 2017, useful for dating protest against named biennials and museums.
If You Don’t Have Bread, Eat Art!: Contemporary Art and Derivative Fascisms

Steyerl argues that art works as an alternative currency valued through gossip, networks and insider influence, tied to inequality, tax avoidance and rising authoritarianism. She points to bank, fossil-fuel and weapons money around art and proposes cooperative circulation instead of speculation.
It frames sponsorship and market value as one system of money and influence, and names Liberate Tate, Gulf Labor and W.A.G.E. as responses.

Steyerl argues that contemporary art screens how war, tax havens and deregulated finance fracture time and space. She calls freeport vaults secret extraterritorial museums, presents a Syrian heritage foundation as regime public relations, and criticises the Louvre's franchising in autocracies.
Louvre, Geneva Freeport, Syria Heritage Foundation
It adds tax-free freeport storage and state-linked cultural patronage to the picture of who pays for art and who benefits.

Öğüt describes how artists withdrew from the 2014 Biennale of Sydney to protest its founding sponsor's role in Australian asylum-seeker detention, and how that pressure led to the sponsor being dropped and the chair resigning.
A documented case where artist withdrawals forced a biennale to cut a sponsor, directly relevant to the map's Biennale of Sydney entry.
Post–Sharjah Biennial 10: Institutional Grease and Institutional Critique

Saadawi argues that the fallout from Sharjah Biennial 10 should widen into a critique of how institutions and capital shape art, beyond boycotts alone. She questions the Sharjah Art Foundation's conduct and state funding, and the Guggenheim's censorship of Hans Haacke in 1971.
Sharjah Art Foundation, Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, Guggenheim
An early (2011) account of how a Gulf state-funded foundation and the boycott call against Guggenheim Abu Dhabi fit into a wider critique of institutions and capital.
Tanja Ostojić's Institutional Gendered Critique Through a Sculptural Lens
texts on the artist Tanja Ostojić

Ekstrand reads I'll Be Your Angel (2001), in which Ostojić shadowed curator Harald Szeemann at the 49th Venice Biennale, and her Curator Series as critique of gendered power between artists and curators. She notes Szeemann never worked with her again. The text discusses no money.
It records how one curator's gatekeeping can end an artist's access to a major biennale; it says nothing on funding or on the Biennale's governance.
Artists from Eastern Europe in Berlin: Tanja Ostojić
texts on the artist Tanja Ostojić

Ostojić says artists in the post-Yugoslav states mostly work without budgets unless close to government, and that German support, including the Goethe-Institut Belgrade, let her show her Lexicon project in four museums there. She adds that passport and residency status shape who gets funded.
It gives an artist's account of how national funders and German cultural diplomacy decided which museums could host her work.
Censorship of Tanja Ostojić's art project at the Q21 exhibition space in MQ Vienna, Austria
texts on the artist Tanja Ostojić

Ostojić says Q21 gave her no written concept or budget, dropped her guest-worker anniversary project for lack of funds, and barred outdoor posters and institutional logos while the interior minister was to speak at the opening. She withdrew, citing censorship and opaque exhibition budgets.
It is her account only, and no reply from Q21 was found; it ties a state-linked show to a cut budget and withheld publicity for one artist.
15 Artists, Shows, and Works Censored in 2016
texts on the artist Tanja Ostojić

Batycka lists the Q21 case as the artists' allegation: Ostojić and Alexander Nikolić say their budget was suspended and they got no promotion after Sebastian Kurz was announced to speak at the opening. He reports it through their account and ArtLeaks, without confirming it.
An independent outlet carries the claim and labels it an allegation, which is how a funding map should treat an unconfirmed account of censorship.
Postidentity and the Aesthetics of Affect in the Work of Tanja Ostojić
texts on the artist Tanja Ostojić

Videkanić argues that Ostojić's work questions where the female body sits within immigration offices, welfare offices, schools and international art organisations. In Be My Guest and I'll Be Your Angel she stages curator and artist relations, exposing institutional power games and Western condescension.
It reads her projects with curators as studies of who holds power in exhibition-making, not of money, and adds the access question to a funding map.
['https://casopiskultura.rs/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/prevodi/1. Bojana Videkanic - Postidentity and the Aesthetics of Affect in the Work of Tanja Ostojic.pdf']
Strategies of Success / Curators Series 2001-2003, introduction
texts on the artist Tanja Ostojić

Ostojić says the series, shown in full only at La BOX in Bourges in October and November 2003, analyses class relations in the art system and relations of power and sexuality from a radically different angle. She judged it too little seen.
It places class and power inside the art system, which a funding map can show only indirectly; it names no funder or institution on the map.

title: The Tear Gas Biennial: Warren B. Kanders and the 2019 Whitney Biennial
kick: Case study. Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, 2018 to 2022.
summary: In November 2018 Hyperallergic linked Whitney vice chair Warren B. Kanders to Safariland tear gas fired at migrants on the US-Mexico border.
Staff, Decolonize This Place and artists pressed the museum for months, and Forensic Architecture used its Biennial slot to investigate Safariland munitions.
After eight artists asked to withdraw their work in July 2019, Kanders resigned from the board on 25 July 2019.
bullets: Kanders resigned from the Whitney board on 25 July 2019.
About two-thirds of roughly 75 Biennial participants signed a letter calling for his removal.
Safariland announced in June 2020 that it would sell Defense Technology (about 8% of sales).
In 2022 The Intercept found the tear gas unit still sat under Kanders's Cadre Holdings.
Brown University revised its gift acceptance policy in October 2019.

timeline.event: Hyperallergic reports that tear gas canisters used at the San Diego-Tijuana (San Ysidro) border carried Safariland markings, linking them to Kanders.
Around 100 Whitney staff sign a letter asking the museum to respond to Kanders's role.
Director Adam Weinberg replies to staff; Kanders writes his own letter defending himself.
Decolonize This Place holds its first protest at the museum; Michael Rakowitz declines to take part in the Biennial.
Decolonize This Place runs nine weekly protests demanding Kanders's removal.
Biennial opens with Forensic Architecture's Triple-Chaser, tracing Safariland munitions and probing Sierra Bullets' possible link to Israeli gunfire at the Gaza fence.
Artforum publishes Hannah Black, Ciarán Finlayson and Tobi Haslett's essay 'The Tear Gas Biennial'.
Korakrit Arunanondchai, Meriem Bennani and Nicole Eisenman write to curators Rujeko Hockley and Jane Panetta asking to withdraw; Nicholas Galanin joins.
Eddie Arroyo, Christine Sun Kim, Agustina Woodgate and Forensic Architecture also ask to withdraw, making eight.
Kanders resigns as Whitney vice chair; his wife Allison leaves her committee co-chair role.
After student protests, Brown University changes its gift acceptance policy (Kanders sat on an advisory council there).
Safariland announces it will divest Defense Technology, its tear gas and crowd-control unit, to that unit's management.
The Intercept reports Kanders still profits from tear gas; Defense Technology and Safariland both sit under his Cadre Holdings.

title: What WikiLeaks shows
kick: Case study. 49 documents on 44 institutions on the map, from leaks covering 1975 to 2016.
summary: We searched the WikiLeaks archive twice: once for every institution on the map, and again for the funders behind the flags, from oil and arms companies to oligarch patrons and Gulf cultural bodies. That covered the US diplomatic cables, the Stratfor emails, the Sony, Podesta and Clinton emails and the Saudi Cables.

The documents mostly confirm what public records already show. They add three things: who paid for two Moscow museums, how Gulf states used museums in their diplomacy, and how the US government treated art it had paid for at the 2008 Biennale of Sydney.

Two pins change tier. The Jewish Museum and Tolerance Center gains a sanctions flag, from a 2008 cable naming Roman Abramovich as a funder. Ithra gains a Gulf state body flag, from a 2009 cable on King Abdullah's project run by state-owned Aramco.

The second pass adds the Koch gifts to Lincoln Center, the American Museum of Natural History, the Met and the Smithsonian, laid out in a profile forwarded in Clinton's email; the 2010 removal of a Wojnarowicz video from the National Portrait Gallery in Washington after a Catholic League complaint; and the Occidental Petroleum ties of the Hammer Museum.

The archive holds nothing on Epstein at any museum, nothing on the Sacklers, Kanders, BAE, Lockheed or Elbit as museum funders, and nothing on the Kennedy Center's funding. Many entries are news reports forwarded inside leaked emails rather than leaked analysis, and the table says so.
